### Pattern 215 — PactFlow RBAC-Gated AI Feature Rollout with CI Code Review Gate [official]

**Description:** PactFlow introduced fine-grained RBAC in 2025 to allow teams to pilot AI features — AI Code Review, AI Test Templates, and the MCP Server — before enabling them org-wide. The recommended rollout pattern is: (1) create a dedicated PactFlow team with AI features enabled for a pilot consumer-provider pair, (2) run AI Code Review in CI and parse its JSON output for quality metrics, (3) expand to additional teams only after the pilot's average matcher specificity score meets the defined threshold. The AI Code Review report includes fields that can be parsed in CI to gate PRs: `overSpecifiedMatchers` (exact values that should use `like()`), `missingErrorInteractions` (endpoints without 4xx coverage), and `providerStateDriftRisk`. Teams that skip the pilot and enable AI features org-wide immediately find that AI-generated tests over-specify matchers in roughly 40% of cases (community observation), creating brittle contracts that block valid provider deployments.

**Use when:** rolling out AI-assisted contract test generation across a large engineering organization where quality consistency is a requirement. **Do NOT use when:** the team is small (< 5 engineers) and direct PR review of pact tests is practical — the RBAC overhead and AI review latency are not worth it. **Alternative:** a custom ESLint rule or PR checklist enforcing `like()` on all ID/timestamp fields is a zero-cost alternative for teams without access to PactFlow's AI tier.

```typescript
// scripts/check-pact-ai-review.ts — CI gate: fail if AI review finds quality issues
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

interface PactAIReviewReport {
  overSpecifiedMatchers: number;    // matchers that should be like() but use exact values
  missingErrorInteractions: number; // endpoints missing ≥1 error-scenario interaction
  providerStateDriftRisk: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high';
}

const THRESHOLDS = {
  overSpecifiedMatchers: 5,
  missingErrorInteractions: 3,
  maxProviderStateDriftRisk: 'medium' as const,
};

async function checkPactAIReview(pactFilePath: string): Promise<void> {
  // PactFlow AI Code Review CLI — available in PactFlow Enterprise tier
  const raw = execSync(
    `pactflow ai-review --pact-file "${pactFilePath}" --output json`,
    { encoding: 'utf-8' },
  );
  const report: PactAIReviewReport = JSON.parse(raw);

  const riskOrder = { low: 0, medium: 1, high: 2 } as const;
  const failures: string[] = [];

  if (report.overSpecifiedMatchers > THRESHOLDS.overSpecifiedMatchers) {
    failures.push(
      `overSpecifiedMatchers=${report.overSpecifiedMatchers} > threshold ${THRESHOLDS.overSpecifiedMatchers}. ` +
      `Replace exact values with like() for IDs, timestamps, and server-assigned fields.`,
    );
  }
  if (riskOrder[report.providerStateDriftRisk] > riskOrder[THRESHOLDS.maxProviderStateDriftRisk]) {
    failures.push(`providerStateDriftRisk=${report.providerStateDriftRisk} exceeds threshold.`);
  }
  if (failures.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(`[pact-ai-review] Quality gate failed:\n  - ${failures.join('\n  - ')}`);
  }
  console.log('[pact-ai-review] Passed.', JSON.stringify(report));
}

checkPactAIReview(process.argv[2]).catch((err) => {
  console.error(err.message);
  process.exit(1);
});
```

### Pattern 216 — `pending(true)` + `includeWipPactsSince` for Safe Parallel Feature Development [official]

**Description:** When a consumer team publishes a pact from a feature branch before the provider has implemented the corresponding endpoint, marking the interaction as `pending: true` prevents it from breaking the provider's main-branch CI. The `VerifierV3` option `includeWipPactsSince` (a date string, e.g., `'2026-01-01'`) tells the Broker to include all "work-in-progress" pacts — pacts from feature branches that have never had a passing provider verification on the provider's main branch — published since that date. These WIP interactions are treated as pending: they can fail without breaking the build, but their results are visible in the Broker for consumer-provider coordination. Together, `enablePending: true` and `includeWipPactsSince` implement the "Pact Nirvana" workflow that allows multiple consumer teams to develop features in parallel without blocking each other or the provider's deployment pipeline.

**Use when:** multiple consumer teams are developing features in parallel that require new provider endpoints, and you want provider CI to stay green while providing early feedback on upcoming contract requirements. **Do NOT use when:** all consumer work happens on main-branch and is coordinated with provider releases — the pending overhead adds configuration complexity with no benefit. **Alternative:** `filterConsumerNames` to temporarily exclude a consumer's new pact from provider CI until the provider implements the endpoint, then remove the filter — simpler but requires manual intervention.

```typescript
// provider-verification-nirvana.ts — full Pact Nirvana VerifierV3 configuration
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

describe('InventoryService — provider verification (Pact Nirvana)', () => {
  it('verifies all current + WIP pacts', async () => {
    jest.setTimeout(120_000);

    const verifier = new VerifierV3({
      provider: 'InventoryService',
      providerBaseUrl: process.env.PROVIDER_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN,
      consumerVersionSelectors: [
        { mainBranch: true },
        { deployedOrReleased: true },
        { matchingBranch: true, fallbackBranch: 'main' },
      ],
      // Include WIP pacts (feature branch pacts never verified on provider main).
      // Published on or after this date — set to project start or last major refactor.
      includeWipPactsSince: '2026-01-01',
      // Pending: WIP + any interaction explicitly marked pending(true) by the consumer.
      // Pending interactions can fail without failing the build; results still published.
      enablePending: true,
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim(),
      stateHandlers: {
        'SKU ABC-123 exists with 10 units': async () => { /* seed */ },
      },
    });

    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

---

### Pattern 217 — `arrayContains` for Polymorphic / Discriminated-Union Response Arrays [official]

**Description:** `MatchersV3.arrayContains([...variants])` is designed for responses that return a heterogeneous array where different elements conform to different schemas (a discriminated union distinguished by a `type` or `kind` field). Rather than asserting that all elements match a single schema (as `eachLike` does), `arrayContains` verifies that each variant definition appears at least once in the actual array. This is the correct matcher for event streams, activity logs, or search result APIs that return mixed item types. Using `eachLike` on a polymorphic array over-constrains the contract: it asserts that every element matches the first element's schema, causing provider verification to fail on legitimate responses where item 2 has a different shape from item 1.

**Use when:** the consumer's API returns a polymorphic array (discriminated union by a `type` field) and the consumer code path depends on multiple distinct variant shapes being present. **Do NOT use when:** the array is homogeneous (all elements have the same schema) — `eachLike` is the correct and simpler choice. **Alternative:** test each variant as a separate interaction (`given('provider has a CREATED event')`, `given('provider has a DELETED event')`) to keep each interaction's scope minimal, avoiding `arrayContains` entirely.

```typescript
// event-stream-consumer.pact.spec.ts — arrayContains for polymorphic event array
import path from 'path';
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { arrayContains, like, string, timestamp } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'EventDashboard',
  provider: 'EventService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('EventDashboard → EventService — polymorphic event stream', () => {
  it('handles CREATED and DELETED event variants in the same response array', async () => {
    await provider
      .addInteraction()
      .given('EventService has recent CREATED and DELETED events')
      .uponReceiving('a GET request for recent events (polymorphic array)')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/events/recent' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        body: {
          // arrayContains: array must contain at least one element matching each variant.
          // Does NOT require all elements to match the same schema (unlike eachLike).
          events: arrayContains([
            // Variant 1: CREATED event — has 'payload' field
            {
              type: string('CREATED'),
              entityId: like('ENT-001'),
              occurredAt: timestamp("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX", '2026-05-14T10:00:00+00:00'),
              payload: like({ name: 'Widget Pro', sku: 'SKU-X' }),
            },
            // Variant 2: DELETED event — has 'deletedBy' field, no 'payload'
            {
              type: string('DELETED'),
              entityId: like('ENT-002'),
              occurredAt: timestamp("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX", '2026-05-14T11:00:00+00:00'),
              deletedBy: like('admin-user'),
            },
          ]),
        },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/events/recent`);
        const data = (await res.json()) as { events: Array<{ type: string }> };
        const types = data.events.map((e) => e.type);
        expect(types).toContain('CREATED');
        expect(types).toContain('DELETED');
      });
  });
});
```

---

### Pattern 218 — `MatchersV3.boolean()` for Strict JSON Boolean Type on Feature-Flag Fields [official]

**Description:** Provider APIs commonly include boolean feature-flag fields in their responses (`isEligible`, `featureEnabled`, `requiresApproval`). Using `like(true)` on a boolean field asserts type-`boolean` — correct in most cases. However, `like()` on a boolean does not prevent the provider from returning a string `"true"` or a number `1` from a misconfigured JSON serialiser. `MatchersV3.boolean(true)` uses the Pact specification's explicit `boolean` type rule, which rejects truthy non-boolean values at the pact-core FFI layer. This makes the contract precisely express the consumer's expectation: the field must be a JSON boolean primitive, not a coerced string or integer. The distinction matters most for consumers that use strict equality checks (`=== true` or `=== false`) rather than truthy coercion.

**Use when:** the consumer's branching logic uses strict equality (`=== true` / `=== false`) on a boolean field and would break silently if the provider returned `"true"` (string) due to serializer misconfiguration. **Do NOT use when:** the consumer's code uses truthy coercion (`!!value` or `if (value)`) — `like(true)` is sufficient and less strict. **Alternative:** `regex(/^true|false$/, 'true')` for legacy APIs that serialise booleans as string literals rather than JSON booleans.

```typescript
// eligibility-consumer.pact.spec.ts — boolean() for strict feature-flag type enforcement
import path from 'path';
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { boolean, like, string } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'CheckoutService',
  provider: 'EligibilityService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('CheckoutService → EligibilityService — boolean feature flags', () => {
  it('returns strict JSON boolean eligibility flags for user USR-001', async () => {
    await provider
      .addInteraction()
      .given('user USR-001 is eligible for express checkout')
      .uponReceiving('a GET request for eligibility flags for USR-001 (strict boolean types)')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/eligibility/USR-001' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        body: {
          userId: string('USR-001'),
          // boolean() enforces JSON boolean primitive — rejects "true" string or 1 integer
          expressCheckoutEnabled:  boolean(true),
          loyaltyDiscountEligible: boolean(false),
          requiresAgeVerification: boolean(false),
          accountSuspended:        boolean(false),
          // Non-boolean fields use like() as usual
          discountPercent: like(10),
          tier: string('GOLD'),
        },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/eligibility/USR-001`);
        const flags = (await res.json()) as Record<string, unknown>;
        // Consumer uses strict equality — depends on JSON boolean, not truthy value
        expect(flags['expressCheckoutEnabled']).toBe(true);
        expect(typeof flags['expressCheckoutEnabled']).toBe('boolean');
      });
  });
});
```

---

### Pattern 219 — `mainBranch` Pacticipant Property Misconfiguration Diagnosis [official]

**Description:** Pending pact status depends on the consumer having its `mainBranch` property set in the Pact Broker. When a consumer publishes pacts from `main` but the Broker's pacticipant record for that consumer has no `mainBranch` configured, pacts published from `main` are never promoted out of "pending" status — every verification result is treated as pending, and `can-i-deploy` returns "unknown compatibility" indefinitely for that consumer. This is silent: the provider CI stays green (pending interactions don't fail the build), but the compatibility gate never clears. Diagnosing this requires checking the Broker's pacticipant configuration, not the pact verification logs. The `pact-broker describe-version` CLI command and the `create-or-update-pacticipant` command are the correct tools for diagnosis and remediation respectively.

**Use when:** debugging a situation where `can-i-deploy` returns "unknown" for a consumer-provider pair even after multiple successful provider verification runs. **Do NOT use when:** `mainBranch` is already configured — this is a one-time setup check. **Alternative:** add `create-or-update-pacticipant` as an idempotent step in every consumer's first CI run to prevent this misconfiguration from occurring in the first place.

```typescript
// scripts/ensure-pacticipant-setup.ts — idempotent; run in consumer CI before publishing
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

interface PacticipantConfig {
  name: string;
  mainBranch: string;    // e.g. 'main' — exact Broker branch name
  displayName?: string;
}

function ensurePacticipant(config: PacticipantConfig): void {
  const brokerUrl   = process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL   ?? '';
  const brokerToken = process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN ?? '';

  const cmd = [
    'pact-broker create-or-update-pacticipant',
    `--name "${config.name}"`,
    `--main-branch "${config.mainBranch}"`,
    config.displayName ? `--display-name "${config.displayName}"` : '',
    `--broker-base-url "${brokerUrl}"`,
    `--broker-token "${brokerToken}"`,
  ].filter(Boolean).join(' ');

  console.log(`[pact] Ensuring pacticipant: ${config.name} (mainBranch: ${config.mainBranch})`);
  execSync(cmd, { stdio: 'inherit' });
}

// Run before publishing pacts on every build — create-or-update is idempotent
ensurePacticipant({ name: 'OrderService',     mainBranch: 'main', displayName: 'Order Service' });
ensurePacticipant({ name: 'InventoryService', mainBranch: 'main', displayName: 'Inventory Service' });
```

---

### Pattern 220 — `filterProviderStates` for Domain-Sharded Parallel Provider Verification [official]

**Description:** `VerifierV3`'s `filterProviderStates` option accepts a string matched as a substring against each interaction's provider state. This allows splitting a large provider verification suite into CI matrix jobs partitioned by resource domain — for example, one job verifies interactions whose provider state contains `'order'`, another `'inventory'`, a third `'user'`. Each job runs in parallel on separate CI workers, reducing wall-clock time proportionally. The approach requires provider state names to follow a consistent domain-prefix convention (`'order: ORD-123 exists'`, `'inventory: SKU ABC-123 has 10 units'`) agreed between consumer and provider teams at the time of writing. This convention should be documented in the project's CONTRIBUTING guide to prevent new consumer developers from omitting the prefix.

**Use when:** provider verification runtime exceeds 10 minutes due to a large interaction count, and interactions can be cleanly partitioned by domain-prefixed provider state names. **Do NOT use when:** provider states are not consistently prefixed — an uneven partition leaves some interactions in no shard and they are never verified. **Alternative:** `filterConsumerNames` partitions by consumer rather than domain, which is preferable when consumers are already team-aligned and one team owns one consumer service.

```typescript
// provider-verification-shard.ts — single shard; run as CI matrix job per domain
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

// CI matrix: strategy.matrix.shard: ['order', 'inventory', 'user', 'payment']
const domainShard = (process.env.DOMAIN_SHARD ?? process.argv[2] ?? 'order').trim();

describe(`InventoryService — provider verification (shard: ${domainShard})`, () => {
  it(`verifies ${domainShard}-domain interactions`, async () => {
    jest.setTimeout(120_000);

    const verifier = new VerifierV3({
      provider: 'InventoryService',
      providerBaseUrl: process.env.PROVIDER_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN,
      consumerVersionSelectors: [
        { mainBranch: true },
        { deployedOrReleased: true },
      ],
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim(),
      // Shard: only verify interactions whose provider state contains the domain prefix.
      // Convention: provider state names must start with '<domain>: <description>'
      // e.g. 'order: ORD-123 exists in PENDING state'
      //      'inventory: SKU ABC-123 has 10 units available'
      filterProviderStates: `${domainShard}:`,
      stateHandlers: {
        // Only handlers for this shard need to be populated per job
        [`${domainShard}: `]: async (_params) => { /* placeholder */ },
      },
    });

    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

### Community Production Lessons — Cycle 35 [community]

188. **[community] Provider verification against `pactUrls` pointing to a local pact file does not publish verification results to the Broker even when `publishVerificationResult: true` is set — results are silently discarded.** Teams debugging a single failing interaction use `pactUrls` to point the verifier at a local copy of the pact file for faster iteration, then forget to revert to `pactBrokerUrl` before merging to main. Because `publishVerificationResult: true` appears in the shared CI config, they expect the Broker to record a passing verification — but pact-js v16 does not publish results when `pactUrls` is used (the local file has no Broker-tracked version to associate results with). The Broker continues to show "unknown" compatibility, `can-i-deploy` fails on the next consumer deployment, and the team investigates why verification "passed in CI" but blocked the gate. **Why it matters:** the local debugging shortcut is correct and useful; the defect is in leaving `pactUrls` active when merging. **Fix:** guard the two options with an environment variable: `pactUrls` only when `LOCAL_PACT_DEBUG=true`, always `pactBrokerUrl` when `CI=true`. [community]

189. **[community] `VerifierV3`'s `beforeEach` / `afterEach` lifecycle hooks fire once per interaction replay — not once per Jest `it` block — causing database teardown functions to run between interactions and leave the provider in an inconsistent state for subsequent interactions.** Teams that write `afterEach: async () => db.clearAll()` expect it to run after each Jest test. In pact-js v16, `beforeEach` / `afterEach` in `VerifierV3` are provider verification lifecycle hooks that fire around each interaction replay within a single `it` block. `db.clearAll()` therefore fires between interaction 1 and interaction 2, wiping state that interaction 2's state handler may not fully reseed. If two interactions share a dependency (e.g., both require a common parent user record), the second interaction's state handler must explicitly reseed that record — it cannot assume it still exists from the previous iteration. **Why it matters:** interactions fail non-deterministically depending on replay order (which can vary between Broker fetches). **Fix:** move teardown logic out of `afterEach` and into the `teardown` action of each individual state handler — tear down only what that handler seeded, never everything. [community]

190. **[community] `can-i-deploy` returns "deployment blocked" when `record-deployment` was called with the wrong environment name (e.g., `'prod'` instead of `'production'`), because the Pact Broker treats environment names as case-sensitive exact strings and creates a new environment entity if the name does not match an existing one.** The Broker creates two separate environment records (`'prod'` and `'production'`), each with their own deployment histories. Consumer version selectors using `{ environment: 'production' }` look up by the exact registered name; if the latest provider deployment was recorded under `'prod'`, the selector finds zero deployed provider versions in `'production'` and `can-i-deploy` returns "unknown" rather than "compatible". **Why it matters:** a misspelled environment name silently decouples deployment records from version selectors — `can-i-deploy` blocks all consumer deployments for that environment without indicating the root cause. **Fix:** centralise environment name constants in a shared CI helper and run `pact-broker list-environments` as a CI check after any infrastructure change; document the exact registered names in the project CONTRIBUTING guide. [community]

191. **[community] The `providerVersionBranch` option in `VerifierV3` must exactly match the branch name that the consumer's `matchingBranch: true` selector resolves to — a `refs/heads/` prefix, trailing newline, or unexpected casing causes `matchingBranch` to find no matching consumer pacts, silently reducing the verified pact set.** Teams that populate `providerVersionBranch` from CI environment variables discover that some CI systems (GitLab CI, older Jenkins pipelines) set the branch variable to `refs/heads/feature/FOO` rather than `feature/FOO`, or that `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` returns a trailing newline when the output is not trimmed. The `matchingBranch` selector finds no consumer pact from the matching branch name and silently skips WIP pact verification — the interaction is not verified, no failure is reported, and the consumer's feature-branch pact accumulates as "unverified" in the Broker, breaking the Pact Nirvana feedback loop. **Why it matters:** the consumer team sees "not verified" in the Broker UI and cannot confirm their feature branch contract is compatible before merging. **Fix:** always normalise `providerVersionBranch`: `process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim()`. [community]

192. **[community] `addAsynchronousInteraction()` consumer tests that omit `.withMetadata({ contentType: 'application/json' })` produce pact files that skip structured body matching during provider verification — the verifier treats the message body as opaque bytes and validates byte count only, not structure.** In pact-js v16, the asynchronous message pact format requires a `contentType` entry in the message metadata block to instruct the pact-core FFI verifier to parse the body as JSON and apply matching rules. When `.withMetadata()` is omitted, the metadata block is empty, and the FFI falls back to byte-length comparison. A consumer test that uses `eachLike`, `like`, and `string` matchers on the message body passes locally (matchers resolve to example values), but provider verification accepts any body with the same byte count — including a body with entirely wrong field names. **Why it matters:** incorrect async message payloads pass provider verification, giving false confidence that the message contract is satisfied. **Fix:** always call `.withMetadata({ contentType: 'application/json' })` (or the correct MIME type) on every async message interaction; add this as a required checklist item in PR reviews for all `addAsynchronousInteraction` usage. [community]

193. **[community] Calling `verifier.verifyProvider()` without `await` inside a Jest `it` block causes the test to pass immediately before verification completes, and Jest process exit aborts the Broker HTTP call mid-flight — leaving the Broker in "verification not published" state and producing a corrupted pact-core log file.** This mistake appears in code copied from documentation examples that omit `await` for brevity. Jest marks the `it` block as passing synchronously (the Promise is returned but never awaited), and without `--detectOpenHandles` the test runner exits silently while the FFI native layer is still writing results. The Broker API call to publish verification results is aborted mid-request, the Broker shows "not verified", and `can-i-deploy` blocks the next consumer deployment. **Why it matters:** CI shows green, the Broker shows "not verified", and the cause is invisible in the test output because the unhandled rejection is swallowed by Jest process exit. **Fix:** always `await verifier.verifyProvider()`; wrap it in `try/catch` to surface rejected Promises as explicit test failures rather than unhandled rejections. [community]

### Pattern 221 — pact-js v16.3.0 Interaction Metadata: `pending`, `comments`, and `testName` Annotations [official]

Pact-js v16.3.0 (March 2026) introduced first-class support for attaching `pending` status, human-readable `comments`, and a `testName` label directly to V4 interactions. These annotations are stored in the generated pact file and are surfaced in the PactFlow UI and Broker API, allowing teams to tag specific interactions as work-in-progress without enabling the global `includeWipPactsSince` flag. The `testName` field records the test function name that produced the interaction, which helps pinpoint the source interaction in large pact files during provider verification failures. `comments` accept an array of strings and are stored under the `comments.text` key in the pact JSON, providing a lightweight changelog for each interaction. Together these fields form a structured annotation model that bridges consumer test intent to provider verification observability.

**Tradeoff:** `pending: true` on an individual interaction gates only that interaction from blocking provider CI — if you also have `enablePending: true` globally, the provider may silently skip verifying the interaction without any warning unless you monitor the Broker UI for "pending" badges. Over-using interaction-level pending can mask a provider's failure to implement new contracts promptly.

```typescript
// order-consumer.pact.spec.ts — interaction-level pending + testName + comments
import { Pact, Matchers } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { OrderClient } from '../src/order-client';

const provider = new Pact({
  consumer: 'OrderConsumer',
  provider: 'OrderService',
  port: 8082,
});

describe('OrderClient — draft bulk-cancel endpoint', () => {
  beforeAll(() => provider.setup());
  afterAll(() => provider.finalize());

  it('handles bulk cancellation response (WIP — endpoint not yet implemented)', async () => {
    await provider
      .addInteraction({
        state: 'orders ORD-1, ORD-2 exist in PENDING state',
        uponReceiving: 'a bulk cancel request for two orders',
        // v16.3.0 metadata annotations
        pending: true,
        comments: ['Endpoint not yet implemented by provider', 'See JIRA PLAT-4821'],
        testName: 'handles bulk cancellation response (WIP)',
        withRequest: {
          method: 'POST',
          path: '/orders/bulk-cancel',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: { orderIds: Matchers.eachLike('ORD-1') },
        },
        willRespondWith: {
          status: 202,
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: {
            cancelled: Matchers.eachLike({ id: Matchers.like('ORD-1'), status: 'CANCELLED' }),
            failed: Matchers.eachLike({ id: Matchers.like('ORD-2'), reason: Matchers.like('NOT_FOUND') }),
          },
        },
      });

    const client = new OrderClient('http://localhost:8082');
    const result = await client.bulkCancel(['ORD-1', 'ORD-2']);
    expect(result.cancelled).toHaveLength(1);
  });
});
```

### Pattern 222 — pact-protobuf-plugin v0.8.0: Embedded `protoc` Compiler (No External Tool Required) [official]

The `pact-protobuf-plugin` v0.8.0 (May 2026) embeds the `protox` crate as its Protocol Buffer compiler, eliminating the requirement for an external `protoc` binary on the build host. Previously, CI pipelines had to install `protoc` via a package manager or a dedicated setup step; any version mismatch between the installed `protoc` and the proto files caused silent schema-parse failures during pact verification. With v0.8.0, the plugin bundles a compatible compiler version, which makes the plugin viable in air-gapped environments, self-hosted Kubernetes runners, and architectures that lack a pre-built `protoc` distribution. The `protocVersion` and `downloadUrl` fields in the plugin manifest are silently ignored (they were previously used to specify an external compiler download). Additionally, the `arrayContains` matcher now works on repeated protobuf fields, enabling assertions that a repeated field contains at least one element matching a pattern rather than requiring an exact field-by-field comparison.

**Tradeoff:** Bundling the compiler increases the plugin binary size by roughly 8–12 MB. For teams with strict artifact size limits or tight network-transfer constraints on CI agents, this trade is worthwhile for the removal of the external dependency; however, teams should update their `pact-plugin-driver` configuration to drop any `protocVersion` pin to avoid confusing future maintainers.

```typescript
// grpc-order-consumer.pact.spec.ts — protobuf plugin v0.8.0, no protoc install needed
import { PactV4 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import path from 'path';

// Plugin installed via: pact-plugin-cli -y install https://github.com/pactflow/pact-protobuf-plugin/releases/tag/v0.8.0
const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'GrpcOrderConsumer',
  provider: 'GrpcOrderService',
  spec: 4,
  logLevel: 'warn',
  pactfileWriteMode: 'merge',
  dir: path.resolve('./pacts'),
});

describe('GrpcOrderService contract — v0.8.0 embedded protoc', () => {
  it('verifies repeated field with arrayContains matcher', async () => {
    const interaction = provider
      .addSynchronousMessageInteraction('GetOrderHistory returns recent orders')
      .usingPlugin({ plugin: 'protobuf', version: '0.8.0' })
      .withRequest(
        'core/user',
        '{"pact:proto":"protos/order.proto","pact:message-type":"OrderHistoryRequest","userId":"matching(type,\'U-001\')"}',
      )
      .withResponse(
        'core/user',
        // arrayContains on repeated field `orders`
        `{"pact:proto":"protos/order.proto","pact:message-type":"OrderHistoryResponse","orders":{"pact:match":"arrayContains","variants":[{"orderId":"matching(type,\'ORD-A\')","status":"matching(equalTo,\'PENDING\')"}]}}`,
      );

    await interaction.executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const { createGrpcOrderClient } = await import('../src/grpc-order-client');
      const client = createGrpcOrderClient(mockServer.url);
      const result = await client.getOrderHistory({ userId: 'U-001' });
      expect(result.orders.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
    });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 223 — `mockServerMatchedSuccessfully()` Race Condition Under Parallel Load (pact-core v19.1.0) [official]

A regression introduced in `@pact-foundation/pact-core` v19.1.0 (March 2026, underlying pact-js v16.3.0) causes `mockServerMatchedSuccessfully()` to return `false` even when the mock server correctly received and responded to a matching HTTP request. The root cause is an async write-back path in the native FFI layer: the request-match record is written asynchronously, and if `mockServerMatchedSuccessfully()` is called before the asynchronous write completes (which is more likely under CPU pressure from parallel test runners), the verification method reads a stale empty-matches list. The defect manifests intermittently — sequential test runs pass consistently while parallel Vitest/Jest worker runs fail non-deterministically. Downgrading to pact-js v16.2.0 (which depends on pact-core v18) eliminates the failure entirely, confirming the regression boundary.

**Tradeoff:** The safest short-term workaround is to pin pact-js to v16.2.x and suppress the automated dependency update (add `"pact-foundation/pact-js": "pin"` to your Renovate config, or set a Dependabot ignore rule) until pact-core releases a fix. Alternatively, serialise pact test files via Vitest's `singleFork` pool so only one worker runs pact tests at a time — this trades test-run speed for stability.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — serialize pact tests to avoid pact-core v19 race condition
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globals: true,
    // Run pact spec files in a single fork to prevent parallel mock-server races
    pool: 'forks',
    poolOptions: {
      forks: {
        singleFork: true,   // serialises all pact worker processes
      },
    },
    // Separate pact specs from unit specs to avoid timeout conflicts
    include: ['**/*.pact.spec.ts'],
    testTimeout: 30_000,
    hookTimeout: 15_000,
    // Explicit reporter to surface FFI-level errors hidden by Vitest's default summariser
    reporters: ['verbose'],
  },
});
```

### Pattern 224 — pact-js v16 Internal Test Suite Migration to Vitest (PR #1789) [official]

Pact-js v16 migrated its own internal test suite from Mocha/Chai/Sinon + NYC coverage to Vitest with native V8 coverage in May 2026 (PR #1789, merged May 6, 2026). While this is an internal change, it has a direct implication for consumer project setups: pact-js is now validated under the same Vitest runtime it recommends to consumers, which means Vitest-specific quirks (pool types, `globalThis` patching, ESM module resolution) are caught by the project's own CI rather than discovered by end users. Consumer teams who had been holding off on adopting Vitest due to uncertainty about pact-js compatibility can now adopt it with higher confidence. The migration replaced Chai `expect()` calls with Vitest's assertion library and converted Sinon stubs to `vi.fn()` mock functions throughout 32 test files.

**Tradeoff:** The migration validates pact-js under Vitest's `forks` pool with `singleFork: true`. Teams using Vitest's `threads` pool (the default) may still encounter the pact-core v19.1.0 race condition (Pattern 223) because the official test suite does not run under `threads` mode. Always explicitly configure `pool: 'forks'` when running pact tests under Vitest.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — consumer project aligned with pact-js PR #1789 configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import tsconfigPaths from 'vite-tsconfig-paths';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [tsconfigPaths()],
  test: {
    globals: true,
    environment: 'node',
    // Align pool configuration with pact-js internal CI (forks, singleFork)
    pool: 'forks',
    poolOptions: { forks: { singleFork: true } },
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.pact.spec.ts'],
    },
    include: ['**/*.{spec,test}.ts'],
    testTimeout: 30_000,
  },
});
```

### Pattern 225 — `enablePending` Global Flag vs Interaction-Level `pending: true` — Choosing the Right Scope [official]

Pact supports two granularities of pending semantics: the global `enablePending: true` flag on `VerifierV3` and the per-interaction `pending: true` annotation introduced in pact-js v16.3.0. The global flag causes the provider to fetch and verify all pacts tagged as pending (i.e., pacts whose content has never been successfully verified on the current provider branch), treating their failures as warnings rather than CI errors. The per-interaction annotation, by contrast, marks a specific interaction as pending regardless of its verification history — useful when a provider acknowledges it has not yet implemented one endpoint but has fully implemented all others in the same pact file. Combining both incorrectly (e.g., global flag on AND interaction-level pending on all new interactions) causes all unverified interactions to become non-blocking forever, defeating the feedback loop that Pact Nirvana depends on.

**Tradeoff:** Prefer interaction-level `pending: true` over the global flag when the provider has partially implemented a pact (some interactions done, some not). Use the global `enablePending` flag only in combination with `includeWipPactsSince` to bootstrap new consumer branches into the verification pipeline without blocking provider CI on day one. Never leave `enablePending: true` in the provider verification config permanently; retire it once all consumers have been onboarded.

```typescript
// provider-verify.spec.ts — surgical use of enablePending + includeWipPactsSince
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

describe('OrderService — provider verification', () => {
  it('verifies all consumer pacts with surgical pending scope', async () => {
    const verifier = new VerifierV3({
      provider: 'OrderService',
      providerBaseUrl: process.env.PROVIDER_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
      consumerVersionSelectors: [
        { mainBranch: true },
        { deployedOrReleased: true },
        { matchingBranch: true },   // picks up WIP consumer branches
      ],
      // Global pending: only enables for WIP pacts introduced in the last 30 days
      enablePending: true,
      includeWipPactsSince: new Date(Date.now() - 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString().split('T')[0],
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim(),
    });

    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

---

### Pattern 226 — `consumer` Selector Scoping for Multi-Team Provider Verification [official]

When a provider is consumed by many teams, every PR triggers verification of all consumer pacts — including pacts from teams whose API surface has nothing to do with the PR's changes. The `consumer` property on `ConsumerVersionSelector` restricts verification to pacts from a named consumer, enabling each team's provider CI job to check only the pacts it cares about without the overhead of verifying unrelated consumers. Combined with the `filterProviderStates` pattern (Pattern 220) and a GitHub Actions matrix strategy, this creates a fully parallelised verification pipeline where each job is both consumer-scoped and provider-state-domain-scoped, reducing wall-clock time proportionally to the number of matrix dimensions.

**Tradeoff:** Scoping by `consumer` name in CI jobs requires that the consumer name used in `new Pact({ consumer: '...' })` is stable and matches the consumer name registered in the Broker. Any rename of a consumer pacticipant invalidates the `consumer` selector across all provider jobs that reference it — co-ordinate renames via `pact-broker create-or-update-pacticipant`.

```typescript
// provider-verify-per-consumer.spec.ts — consumer-scoped matrix job
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

// CI env: CONSUMER_NAME = 'CheckoutService' | 'InventoryReader' | 'AdminDashboard'
const consumerName = process.env.CONSUMER_NAME;
if (!consumerName) throw new Error('CONSUMER_NAME must be set');

describe(`OrderService — provider verification for ${consumerName}`, () => {
  it('verifies pacts from the named consumer only', async () => {
    jest.setTimeout(120_000);

    const verifier = new VerifierV3({
      provider: 'OrderService',
      providerBaseUrl: process.env.PROVIDER_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
      consumerVersionSelectors: [
        { mainBranch: true, consumer: consumerName },
        { deployedOrReleased: true, consumer: consumerName },
        { matchingBranch: true, consumer: consumerName },
      ],
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim(),
    });

    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

### Pattern 227 — Pact Nirvana Diamond Level: `record-release` vs `record-deployment` for Non-Ephemeral Artefacts [official]

Pact distinguishes between `record-deployment` (for services deployed to an environment) and `record-release` (for artefacts — libraries, SDKs, npm packages — that are published to a package registry and consumed by multiple dependents independently). Misusing `record-deployment` for a published npm package causes the `can-i-deploy` gate to block the package release because it is waiting for an "undeployment" of the previous version that never comes. The correct model: libraries and packages call `pact-broker record-release --pacticipant <name> --version <ver> --environment production`, which marks the version as "released" rather than "deployed", and the `deployedOrReleased: true` consumer version selector picks it up correctly. Once a library version is superseded, call `pact-broker record-support-ended` to deregister it.

**Tradeoff:** The `record-release` / `record-support-ended` lifecycle requires discipline on the library team's release pipeline. If `record-support-ended` is never called, old library versions accumulate as "released" indefinitely, causing the provider to verify an ever-growing set of pacts. Add `record-support-ended` to the release pipeline as a step triggered N versions after the current release (e.g., when v1.2.0 releases, mark v1.0.0 as support-ended).

```bash
# .github/workflows/library-release.yml (excerpt)
# Step 1: publish npm package
# - name: Publish npm
#   run: npm publish --access public

# Step 2: record release in Pact Broker (NOT record-deployment)
# - name: Record Pact release
#   run: |
pact-broker record-release \
  --pacticipant OrderSdkConsumer \
  --version "$GIT_COMMIT" \
  --environment production \
  --broker-base-url "$PACT_BROKER_URL" \
  --broker-token "$PACT_BROKER_TOKEN"

# Step 3: end support for the version N-3 to avoid accumulation
# OLD_VERSION=$(cat .release-history | tail -n 4 | head -n 1)
pact-broker record-support-ended \
  --pacticipant OrderSdkConsumer \
  --version "$OLD_VERSION" \
  --environment production \
  --broker-base-url "$PACT_BROKER_URL" \
  --broker-token "$PACT_BROKER_TOKEN"
```

### Pattern 228 — `withMatchingRules` for Async and Sync Messages (pact-js v16.2.0) [official]

Pact-js v16.2.0 (February 2026) extended the `withMatchingRules` API to cover both asynchronous message interactions (`addAsynchronousInteraction`) and synchronous message interactions (`addSynchronousMessageInteraction`). Before this release, matching rules on message bodies required indirect workarounds (nesting matchers inside the content body rather than attaching an explicit rules block). The new `withMatchingRules` method accepts a `MatchingRuleCategory` object that mirrors the HTTP body matching rule DSL, giving consumers explicit control over deep-path matching rules without embedding them in the body structure. This is particularly useful when the message schema is generated from a JSON Schema or Protobuf descriptor and the team cannot modify the content object shape.

**Tradeoff:** Explicit `withMatchingRules` declarations duplicate information already present in matcher calls inside the body (e.g., `Matchers.like(...)` already generates a matching rule). Using both simultaneously causes the explicit rules block to override the implicit rules, which can silently weaken matching. Prefer the inline matcher API for most cases; use `withMatchingRules` only when the body schema is externally generated and the content object is not under your control.

```typescript
// inventory-event-consumer.pact.spec.ts — withMatchingRules on async message (v16.2.0+)
import { MessageConsumerPact, Matchers } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const messagePact = new MessageConsumerPact({
  consumer: 'InventoryEventConsumer',
  provider: 'InventoryEventProducer',
  dir: './pacts',
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('InventoryEventConsumer — stock-updated event', () => {
  it('handles stock-updated message with explicit matching rules', () => {
    return messagePact
      .expectsToReceive('a stock-updated event')
      .withMetadata({ contentType: 'application/json', 'x-event-type': 'stock-updated' })
      .withContent({
        // Content generated from external schema — cannot add inline matchers
        skuId: 'SKU-0001',
        warehouseId: 'WH-EAST-01',
        quantityAvailable: 100,
        reservedQuantity: 0,
        updatedAt: '2026-05-14T00:00:00Z',
      })
      .withMatchingRules({
        body: {
          '$.skuId':             { matchers: [{ match: 'type' }] },
          '$.warehouseId':       { matchers: [{ match: 'type' }] },
          '$.quantityAvailable': { matchers: [{ match: 'integer' }] },
          '$.reservedQuantity':  { matchers: [{ match: 'integer' }] },
          '$.updatedAt':         { matchers: [{ match: 'datetime', format: "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssX" }] },
        },
      })
      .verify(async (message) => {
        const event = JSON.parse(message.contents.toString());
        expect(typeof event.skuId).toBe('string');
        expect(typeof event.quantityAvailable).toBe('number');
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 229 — `logLevel: 'error'` Suppression of FFI Noise + Env-Driven Debug Override [community]

Pact-js emits verbose FFI-level log lines (e.g., `[pact_ffi] DEBUG: mock server started on port …`, `[pact_ffi] TRACE: …`) at default log levels, which bloat CI logs and obscure the actual test output. The `logLevel` option on `Pact`, `PactV4`, `MessageConsumerPact`, and `VerifierV3` constructors accepts `'error' | 'warn' | 'info' | 'debug' | 'trace' | 'none'`. Setting `logLevel: 'error'` in all environments and overriding it to `'debug'` via an environment variable only when actively debugging eliminates the noise while preserving the ability to triage FFI crashes in local development.

**Tradeoff:** `logLevel: 'none'` fully silences the FFI layer, including native-layer crash reports. If pact-core itself panics (rare but possible on unsupported OS/arch combinations), there will be no log output to aid diagnosis. Prefer `logLevel: 'error'` over `'none'` in production CI so fatal errors are still surfaced.

```typescript
// pact-config.ts — centralised log level helper for all pact tests in the repo
export const PACT_LOG_LEVEL =
  (process.env.PACT_LOG_LEVEL as 'error' | 'warn' | 'info' | 'debug' | 'trace' | 'none') ??
  (process.env.CI ? 'error' : 'warn');

// order-consumer.pact.spec.ts
import { Pact, Matchers } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { PACT_LOG_LEVEL } from '../test/pact-config';

const provider = new Pact({
  consumer: 'OrderConsumer',
  provider: 'OrderService',
  port: 8083,
  logLevel: PACT_LOG_LEVEL,   // 'error' in CI, 'warn' locally
});

describe('OrderConsumer — get order', () => {
  beforeAll(() => provider.setup());
  afterAll(() => provider.finalize());

  it('fetches a single order by ID', async () => {
    await provider.addInteraction({
      state: 'order ORD-9001 exists',
      uponReceiving: 'a GET request for order ORD-9001',
      withRequest: { method: 'GET', path: '/orders/ORD-9001' },
      willRespondWith: {
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: { id: Matchers.like('ORD-9001'), status: Matchers.like('PENDING') },
      },
    });
    // exercise the real HTTP client…
  });
});
```

### Pattern 230 — Bi-Directional Contract Testing (BDCT) with OpenAPI for Provider-First Teams [official]

PactFlow's Bi-Directional Contract Testing (BDCT) workflow enables contract testing without requiring the provider team to write a Pact verification test. Instead, the provider uploads their OpenAPI specification to PactFlow (`pactflow publish-provider-contract`), and PactFlow performs schema-level compatibility checking between the consumer's pact file and the provider's OpenAPI spec. This is ideal for teams adopting CDC incrementally: the consumer team writes a Pact consumer test as normal (generating a pact file), while the provider team only needs to maintain an accurate OpenAPI spec — no provider verification setup required. PactFlow compares the pact interactions against the OpenAPI paths, request schemas, and response schemas and reports any mismatches in the compatibility matrix.

**Tradeoff:** BDCT checks structural compatibility only — it cannot verify that the provider's implementation actually matches its OpenAPI spec. Teams must run a separate conformance step (e.g., PactFlow Drift, Dredd, or `openapi-backend`) to validate that the running provider matches its uploaded spec. BDCT is therefore a stepping-stone, not a replacement for full Pact verification; use it to unblock teams during migration and retire it in favour of standard Pact once the provider team is fully onboarded.

```bash
# ci/publish-provider-contract.sh — BDCT provider side (no pact-js verifier needed)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Step 1: lint the OpenAPI spec before publishing
npx @apidevtools/swagger-cli validate openapi/order-service.yaml

# Step 2: publish the spec as the provider contract to PactFlow
pactflow publish-provider-contract \
  openapi/order-service.yaml \
  --provider OrderService \
  --provider-app-version "$GIT_COMMIT" \
  --branch "${GIT_BRANCH//refs\/heads\//}" \
  --content-type application/yaml \
  --verification-success \
  --broker-base-url "$PACT_BROKER_URL" \
  --broker-token "$PACT_BROKER_TOKEN"

# Step 3: can-i-deploy — BDCT compatibility check
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant OrderService \
  --version "$GIT_COMMIT" \
  --to-environment production \
  --broker-base-url "$PACT_BROKER_URL" \
  --broker-token "$PACT_BROKER_TOKEN"
```

---

### Pattern 231 — `fallbackBranch` Driven from CI Environment Variable for Non-Standard Default Branches [official]

The `fallbackBranch` property on `ConsumerVersionSelector` is a literal string — it specifies the branch name to fall back to when the primary `branch` selector finds no matching pacts. A common source of confusion is that `mainBranch: true` resolves to the `mainBranch` property registered on the pacticipant in the Broker, while `fallbackBranch: 'main'` is a hardcoded literal. Repositories that use `master`, `trunk`, or `develop` as their default branch name need to pass the actual default branch name as the fallback, not the string `'main'`. The TypeScript type for `ConsumerVersionSelector` does not enforce this: `fallbackBranch` accepts any `string`, so a misconfigured `fallbackBranch: 'main'` on a `master`-default-branch repo compiles without error but silently falls back to a branch that does not exist — returning zero pacts from the fallback selector and producing no CI failure.

**Tradeoff:** The safest approach is to drive `fallbackBranch` from the same CI variable that populates the Broker's `mainBranch` pacticipant registration, keeping both values in sync via a single source of truth rather than a hardcoded string.

```typescript
// consumer-version-selectors.ts — fallbackBranch from shared constant
import type { ConsumerVersionSelector } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

// DEFAULT_BRANCH env var: set in CI; default to 'main' for standard repos only
const DEFAULT_BRANCH = process.env.DEFAULT_BRANCH ?? 'main';

export const standardSelectors: ConsumerVersionSelector[] = [
  { mainBranch: true },
  { deployedOrReleased: true },
  {
    branch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim() ?? DEFAULT_BRANCH,
    fallbackBranch: DEFAULT_BRANCH,  // driven from env, not a hardcoded literal
  },
];

// provider-verify.spec.ts — use the shared selector list
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { standardSelectors } from '../test/consumer-version-selectors';

describe('OrderService provider verification', () => {
  it('verifies with fallback-safe selectors', async () => {
    const verifier = new VerifierV3({
      provider: 'OrderService',
      providerBaseUrl: process.env.PROVIDER_URL!,
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
      consumerVersionSelectors: standardSelectors,
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim(),
    });
    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

### Pattern 232 — PactFlow Drift: Spec-Driven Provider Compliance for BDCT Gap Detection [official]

PactFlow Drift (March 2026) addresses the gap in Bi-Directional Contract Testing: BDCT validates that the consumer's pact is compatible with the provider's OpenAPI spec, but does not validate that the provider's implementation actually conforms to its OpenAPI spec. Drift automates this via CI-native conformance testing — it runs the provider against its uploaded spec using PactFlow's analysis engine and reports "drift" when the live API diverges from the spec. Drift integrates into the `can-i-deploy` compatibility matrix: if Drift detects the running provider does not match its spec, the provider version is flagged as non-conformant and `can-i-deploy` blocks deployments for consumers that depend on the drifted endpoints. This closes the BDCT trust gap without requiring teams to write explicit provider Pact verification tests.

**Tradeoff:** Drift requires the provider to be running (or a deployed environment to be accessible) at the time of the compliance check, unlike standard Pact verification which can run against a locally-started provider in CI. Teams with providers that cannot be run in CI without full infrastructure must either deploy to a staging environment first or fall back to standard Pact verification.

```typescript
// ci/drift-check.ts — trigger Drift compliance check from provider CI
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

function runDriftCheck(): void {
  const provider   = process.env.PROVIDER_NAME   ?? 'OrderService';
  const providerUrl = process.env.PROVIDER_URL   ?? 'http://localhost:3000';
  const version    = process.env.GIT_COMMIT!;
  const brokerUrl  = process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!;
  const token      = process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!;

  // pactflow CLI: run Drift spec-conformance check against running provider
  const cmd = [
    'pactflow drift check',
    `--provider "${provider}"`,
    `--provider-base-url "${providerUrl}"`,
    `--provider-app-version "${version}"`,
    `--broker-base-url "${brokerUrl}"`,
    `--broker-token "${token}"`,
  ].join(' \\\n  ');

  console.log('Running Drift check:', cmd);
  execSync(cmd, { stdio: 'inherit' });
}

runDriftCheck();
```

### Pattern 233 — PactFlow AI Code Review CI Quality Gate with Score-Threshold Enforcement [official]

PactFlow's AI Code Review feature (beta August 2025, GA rollout 2026) analyses pact files for quality issues: over-specified request matchers, missing response matchers, interactions that test business logic rather than contract shape, and interactions with duplicate `uponReceiving` descriptions. The AI review is surfaced in the PactFlow UI per pact file and also via the Broker API, making it consumable in CI pipelines. Teams can add a CI step that fetches the AI review result for newly published pacts and fails the PR if the review score falls below a threshold. The API endpoint is `GET /pacts/provider/:provider/consumer/:consumer/version/:version/ai-review` and returns a `score` (0–100) and `issues` array. RBAC gates which teams have AI Code Review enabled (`ai-review` permission group, configurable since December 2024).

**Tradeoff:** AI Code Review catches semantic issues (e.g., testing too many validation scenarios) that static linting cannot detect, but it adds a network-dependent CI step that requires connectivity to PactFlow. Teams in strict network-segmented CI environments may need to allow-list PactFlow API egress. The score is non-deterministic (LLM-based) and should be used as a guidance gate (warn on score < 70, fail on score < 50) rather than a hard binary pass/fail.

```typescript
// ci/pact-ai-review-gate.ts — quality gate using PactFlow AI Code Review API
import axios from 'axios';

interface AiReviewIssue {
  severity: 'error' | 'warning' | 'info';
  message: string;
  interaction?: string;
}

interface AiReviewResult {
  score: number;
  issues: AiReviewIssue[];
}

async function checkAiReviewGate(
  provider: string,
  consumer: string,
  version: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const brokerUrl = process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!;
  const token     = process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!;

  const { data } = await axios.get<AiReviewResult>(
    `${brokerUrl}/pacts/provider/${provider}/consumer/${consumer}/version/${version}/ai-review`,
    { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } },
  );

  const errors   = data.issues.filter((i) => i.severity === 'error');
  const warnings = data.issues.filter((i) => i.severity === 'warning');

  console.log(`AI Review score: ${data.score}/100 (${errors.length} errors, ${warnings.length} warnings)`);
  errors.forEach((e)   => console.error(`  [ERROR] ${e.interaction ?? ''}: ${e.message}`));
  warnings.forEach((w) => console.warn(`  [WARN]  ${w.interaction ?? ''}: ${w.message}`));

  if (data.score < 50) {
    throw new Error(`Pact AI Review score ${data.score} is below the 50-point failure threshold.`);
  }
  if (data.score < 70) {
    console.warn(`Pact AI Review score ${data.score} is below the 70-point warning threshold.`);
  }
}

await checkAiReviewGate('OrderService', 'CheckoutService', process.env.GIT_COMMIT!);
```

### Pattern 234 — `VerifierV3` Proxy Root Path Fix (pact-js v16.0.1) — Sub-Path `providerBaseUrl` Now Preserved [official]

Pact-js v16.0.1 (October 2025) patched a defect in the `VerifierV3` proxy path handling where providers mounted at a non-root URL path (e.g., `providerBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000/api/v2'`) had the path prefix stripped by the verifier proxy, causing all verification requests to hit `/` instead of `/api/v2/<endpoint>`. The defect only affected provider setups where the base URL contained a path component; providers mounted at the domain root (`http://localhost:3000`) were unaffected. Teams that discovered this defect typically worked around it by launching a path-stripping reverse proxy in front of the test server — this workaround should be removed after upgrading to v16.0.1 or later.

**Tradeoff:** After upgrading and removing the workaround proxy, state handler routes registered at `/pact/provider-state` may need to be updated to ensure they are mounted at the same base path used in `providerBaseUrl`, since the verifier now forwards requests with the full path prefix intact.

```typescript
// provider-verify.spec.ts — provider mounted at sub-path, v16.0.1+ fix applied
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { startProviderApp } from '../src/app';
import type { Server } from 'http';

describe('OrderService provider verification — sub-path mount', () => {
  let server: Server;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    // Provider is mounted at /api/v2 — path now preserved by verifier proxy (v16.0.1+)
    server = await startProviderApp({ port: 3005, basePath: '/api/v2' });
  });

  afterAll(() => { server.close(); });

  it('verifies pacts against /api/v2 base path', async () => {
    const verifier = new VerifierV3({
      provider: 'OrderService',
      // v16.0.1+: path component is no longer stripped by the proxy
      providerBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:3005/api/v2',
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
      consumerVersionSelectors: [{ mainBranch: true }, { deployedOrReleased: true }],
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace(/^refs\/heads\//, '').trim(),
      stateHandlers: {
        'order ORD-001 exists': async () => { /* seed db */ },
      },
    });

    await verifier.verifyProvider();
  });
});
```

### Pattern 235 — `create-or-update-pacticipant` Registration Guard for `mainBranch` and `repositoryUrl` [official]

The Pact Broker stores a `repositoryUrl` property on each pacticipant that the UI uses to generate links back to the source repository and that PactFlow uses to display blame information when verification fails. When a consumer or provider is first registered via publishing (implicitly, the first time a pact is published or verification result is posted), `repositoryUrl` is `null`. Teams that later try to use `matchingBranch` or `mainBranch` selectors discover that these selectors require the `mainBranch` property to be set on the pacticipant — also `null` by default. Both properties must be set explicitly via `pact-broker create-or-update-pacticipant` in the repository's setup step; the pact-js SDK does not set them automatically during pact publishing.

**Tradeoff:** Adding a `create-or-update-pacticipant` step to CI means the Broker must be reachable during every CI run, including ephemeral branch builds. Teams with Broker availability SLAs below 99.9% should add `--retry-while-unknown 3 --retry-interval 10` to the command to tolerate transient outages without failing CI.

```bash
# bin/register-pacticipants.sh — run once per repo setup and on every new pacticipant addition
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

BROKER_URL="${PACT_BROKER_URL}"
TOKEN="${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}"
REPO_URL="https://github.com/my-org/order-platform"
DEFAULT_BRANCH="${DEFAULT_BRANCH:-main}"

for PACTICIPANT in "OrderService" "CheckoutService" "InventoryReader" "AdminDashboard"; do
  pact-broker create-or-update-pacticipant \
    --name "$PACTICIPANT" \
    --main-branch "$DEFAULT_BRANCH" \
    --repository-url "$REPO_URL" \
    --broker-base-url "$BROKER_URL" \
    --broker-token "$TOKEN"
  echo "Registered pacticipant: $PACTICIPANT (mainBranch: $DEFAULT_BRANCH)"
done
```

### Community Production Lessons — Cycle 37 [community]

194. **[community] Publishing a pact with `pactfileWriteMode: 'merge'` when the previous pact file on disk contains interactions from a feature branch that has already been merged and deleted causes the published pact to include stale, zombie interactions that the provider must verify indefinitely.** Teams use `pactfileWriteMode: 'merge'` to accumulate interactions across multiple test files without overwriting the single pact output file. The defect occurs when a developer runs tests locally on a feature branch, the pact file on disk accumulates the branch's interactions, the branch is merged and the feature interactions are removed from the test code — but the developer never runs the tests locally again to regenerate the pact file. The next CI run publishes the stale pact (which still contains deleted interactions from the merged branch) because the local file was checked in or cached. The provider's verification job now fails on interactions that no longer exist in the consumer's source code. **Why it matters:** zombie interactions accumulate silently and can block provider deployments for months until someone manually audits the Broker. **Fix:** always delete the pacts directory before the pact test step in CI (`rimraf pacts/`); in local development, document in the project README that pact directories must be cleared before running tests on a new branch. [community]

195. **[community] `pact-broker can-i-deploy` succeeds with exit code 0 when run against a consumer version that has never published a pact — instead of failing, the command treats an absent pact as "no contract, no constraint" and returns "you can deploy".** Teams expect `can-i-deploy` to act as a hard gate that fails when there is no verified compatibility record. The actual behaviour is documented but frequently misunderstood: if neither side has published a pact or verification result for a given consumer/provider pair, the Pact Broker has no evidence of incompatibility and returns "OK to deploy". This means a consumer whose pact publishing step was accidentally skipped in CI (e.g., the pact-js publisher step ran but wrote no pact file because an environment variable was missing) will pass `can-i-deploy` without any contract safety net. **Why it matters:** the gate appears green but offers zero protection. **Fix:** add a separate CI step that asserts the expected pact files were created (`test -f pacts/ConsumerName-ProviderName.json`) before the `can-i-deploy` call; fail the pipeline if pact files are missing. [community]

196. **[community] Calling `provider.addInteraction()` with a `state` string that contains a trailing space (e.g., `'order ORD-001 exists '`) causes the state handler lookup to fail silently during provider verification — the verifier receives `'order ORD-001 exists '` but the `stateHandlers` map key is `'order ORD-001 exists'`, and JavaScript object key lookup is exact-match with no trim.** This defect appears in tests where the state string is assembled from a template literal or copied from a design document with inadvertent trailing whitespace. The verifier logs `No state handler found for state: order ORD-001 exists ` at WARN level (the trailing space is invisible in most terminal fonts) and proceeds without setting up the required database state. The interaction then fails on a 404 or data-integrity error, and the team spends hours debugging the database seed rather than the state string. **Why it matters:** the root cause is a one-character invisible difference between the consumer pact and the provider state handler key. **Fix:** sanitise all state strings with `.trim()` before passing them to `addInteraction` and before registering `stateHandlers` keys; add a lint rule or test utility that asserts all state strings in all pact files are trimmed. [community]

197. **[community] Using `jest.setTimeout()` inside a `beforeAll()` block (rather than at the top-level `describe` scope) does not apply to the `it` block that contains `verifier.verifyProvider()` — Jest applies the timeout set via `jest.setTimeout()` at the time the `it` block is registered, not at the time `beforeAll` runs, causing large provider suites to hit the default 5-second timeout even when `beforeAll` correctly called `jest.setTimeout(120_000)`.** Teams that follow examples where `jest.setTimeout(120_000)` appears inside `beforeAll` are surprised when provider verification times out in CI despite the seemingly correct configuration. Jest's `setTimeout` only affects tests registered after the call executes synchronously, and `beforeAll` runs after all `it` blocks are registered by the describe callback. **Why it matters:** the test fails with a cryptic timeout error that looks like a provider health or network issue rather than a configuration issue. **Fix:** always call `jest.setTimeout(120_000)` at the top of the `describe` block — before any `it` declarations — or use Vitest's `testTimeout` in `vitest.config.ts` to set a global timeout for pact spec files. [community]

198. **[community] `VerifierV3`'s `requestFilter` middleware receives the raw `IncomingMessage` from Node's `http` module, not an Express `Request` — calling `req.body` inside `requestFilter` always returns `undefined` because the body has not been parsed, causing conditional auth injection that reads `req.body.userId` to silently fall through to the unauthenticated path.** Teams write `requestFilter` handlers that inspect the request body to determine which auth token to inject (e.g., inject admin token if `req.body.role === 'admin'`). The raw `IncomingMessage` has no `body` property populated by default; the handler reads `undefined`, falls through the conditional, and injects no auth header. Provider verification then fails with 401 on interactions that require role-specific tokens. **Why it matters:** `requestFilter` is the idiomatic place for dynamic auth injection in multi-role provider suites, but the missing body parse is a footgun that is not documented in the pact-js API reference. **Fix:** either read the body via `await getRawBody(req)` and parse it manually inside `requestFilter`, or drive auth token selection from the provider state name (which is available as a state handler parameter) rather than the request body. [community]

199. **[community] `Matchers.timestamp()` in pact-js uses Java SimpleDateFormat patterns (e.g., `"yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ"`), not JavaScript `Intl.DateTimeFormat` patterns — using a JavaScript-style pattern (e.g., `"YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ"`) produces a regex that matches the wrong character classes and causes provider verification to accept malformed timestamps.** The Java SimpleDateFormat pattern `yyyy` means a 4-digit year, but a JavaScript-style `YYYY` also compiles without error in pact-js (it is treated as a valid pattern character sequence) and generates a regex that matches literal `Y` characters rather than digits. Consumer tests pass because the example value is generated by the library (which resolves the example correctly from its own parser), but provider verification applies the generated regex to real provider output and silently accepts garbage timestamps. **Why it matters:** the pact file appears valid, the consumer test passes, and provider verification passes — but the contract does not enforce the correct timestamp format. **Fix:** always use Java SimpleDateFormat notation for `Matchers.timestamp()`, `Matchers.date()`, and `Matchers.time()`; add a code comment referencing the Java SimpleDateFormat spec URL to prevent future developers from translating to JavaScript notation. [community]

### Pattern 236 — `matchStatus()` HTTP Response Status Class Matching (PR #1790) [official]

PR #1790 implements the long-requested feature from issue #1600: the ability to apply flexible matching to HTTP response status codes rather than requiring an exact integer match. The implementation introduces `matchStatus(HTTPResponseStatusClass.Success)` which generates a regex-backed matcher that accepts any `2xx` status rather than pinning to `200`. The `HTTPResponseStatusClass` enum exposes `Informational`, `Success`, `Redirect`, `ClientError`, `ServerError`, and `NonError` variants. Internally the implementation requires two separate FFI calls — `withStatus()` sets the example integer value (used by the mock server to respond) and `withResponseMatchingRules()` applies the constraint to provider verification — consistent with how body matchers separate example values from rules.

**Tradeoff:** Using `HTTPResponseStatusClass.Success` in place of a hard-coded `200` reduces false negatives when a provider legitimately returns `201 Created` instead of `200 OK`, but it also allows a provider to return `204 No Content` for a resource-creation endpoint that the consumer's code path expects a body from — the contract will pass while the consumer silently reads an empty body. Pair status class matching with response body matchers to avoid this blind spot.

```typescript
// order-create.consumer.pact.spec.ts
import path from 'path';
import { Pact, MatchersV3, HTTPResponseStatusClass } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const { like, string, integer, matchStatus } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new Pact({
  consumer: 'OrderService',
  provider: 'FulfillmentService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  port: 8092,
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('POST /orders — status class matching', () => {
  it('accepts any 2xx status for a successful order creation', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('FulfillmentService is operational')
      .uponReceiving('a POST request to create a new order')
      .withRequest({
        method: 'POST',
        path: '/orders',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: {
          customerId: string('CUST-001'),
          items: [{ sku: string('ABC-123'), qty: integer(2) }],
        },
      })
      .willRespondWith({
        // matchStatus accepts any HTTPResponseStatusClass variant
        status: matchStatus(HTTPResponseStatusClass.Success),
        body: {
          orderId: string('ORD-9001'),
          status: string('pending'),
        },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const client = new OrderClient(mockServer.url);
        const result = await client.createOrder({
          customerId: 'CUST-001',
          items: [{ sku: 'ABC-123', qty: 2 }],
        });
        expect(result.orderId).toBeDefined();
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 237 — XML Body Matching with `XmlBuilder` and Generators (PactV3 / V3 spec) [official]

Pact-JS supports XML request and response bodies through `XmlBuilder`, available for `PactV3` and `MessageConsumerPact` interactions (not `Pact`/`PactV4` consumers or `PactV2`). The `XmlBuilder` constructor takes XML version, encoding, and root element name; child elements are added fluently with `appendElement()` accepting a callback for nesting. Matching rules (`like()`, `regex()`, `integer()`, `timestamp()`) and generators are applied per-element using the same V3 matcher API used for JSON bodies. XML generators were formally merged in 2025 following an RFC, adding text-content and attribute generators so the mock can return dynamic ISO timestamps or IDs that still match the declared format.

**Tradeoff:** `XmlBuilder` generates a JSON-encoded representation of the XML tree that pact-js serialises into the pact file — this means the pact file contains no raw XML, only the DSL tree. Teams that try to read pact files to debug XML shape mismatches will find the tree harder to read than raw XML. The `PactV4`/`Pact` consumer interface does not support `XmlBuilder`, so teams must remain on `PactV3` for XML-heavy service interactions.

```typescript
// product-feed.consumer.pact.spec.ts
import path from 'path';
import { PactV3, XmlBuilder, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { ProductFeedClient } from '../src/product-feed-client';

const { like, string, integer, timestamp } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'CatalogService',
  provider: 'ProductFeedAPI',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  port: 8093,
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('GET /feed.xml — XML body matching', () => {
  it('returns a product feed with matching rules on each element', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('at least one product exists')
      .uponReceiving('a GET request for the product feed')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/feed.xml' })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/xml' },
        body: new XmlBuilder('1.0', 'UTF-8', 'feed').build((feed) => {
          feed.setAttributes({ xmlns: 'http://www.example.com/feed' });
          feed.appendElement('updated', {}, (el) =>
            el.setContent(timestamp("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ", '2026-01-15T10:00:00+0000'))
          );
          feed.appendElement('entry', {}, (entry) => {
            entry.appendElement('id', {}, (el) => el.setContent(string('PROD-001')));
            entry.appendElement('title', {}, (el) => el.setContent(like('Widget Pro')));
            entry.appendElement('price', {}, (el) => el.setContent(integer(1999)));
          });
        }),
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const client = new ProductFeedClient(mockServer.url);
        const feed = await client.getFeed();
        expect(feed.entries).toHaveLength(1);
        expect(feed.entries[0].id).toBeDefined();
      });
  });
});
```
