### Community Production Lessons — Cycle 42 [community]

222. **[community] When `enablePending: true` is set in VerifierV3 but `providerVersionBranch` is omitted from the verification publish call, every pact remains in pending state indefinitely — the Pact Broker uses the branch association of the verification result to determine when a pact "graduates" from pending, and without a branch the graduation logic never triggers.** A pact enters pending status because no successful verification has been published against it for any specific branch. The Broker's pending status is resolved by associating a successful verification result with a branch (via `providerVersionBranch`) and then using that branch in the consumer's version selectors to determine which verification result "counts." If `providerVersionBranch` is absent, the Broker cannot attribute the successful verification to any branch, so the pact never graduates from pending even after the provider successfully verifies it 100 times. **Why it matters:** provider engineers see all pacts as non-blocking forever, and the pending feature provides zero protection against genuine regressions — the team's safety net has a permanent hole. **Fix:** always set both `providerVersion: process.env.GIT_SHA` and `providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH` in the VerifierV3 config; add a pre-verification assertion that both env vars are truthy in CI. [community]

223. **[community] Consumer test files that call `new PactV4(...)` with a hardcoded `port` property and are run in parallel with Jest's `--maxWorkers` flag will fail with `EADDRINUSE` because multiple worker processes attempt to start mock servers on the same port simultaneously.** Jest's parallel test runner spawns multiple Node.js worker processes, each loading the test file independently. If every test file configures `new PactV4({ port: 8080 })`, all workers attempt to bind port 8080 concurrently. Only the first worker succeeds; the rest fail with `EADDRINUSE` which Jest reports as a test failure unrelated to the Pact interaction. The error is often misdiagnosed as a Pact framework bug because the stack trace points to `pact.setup()` internals. **Why it matters:** parallelism-related defects appear intermittently depending on worker scheduling — the test suite passes in serial mode (`--runInBand`) and fails randomly in parallel mode, creating a misleading "flaky test" diagnosis. **Fix:** omit the `port` property entirely to allow Pact to assign a random available port; if a fixed port is required, use `process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID` to compute a unique port per worker: `port: 8080 + parseInt(process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID ?? '0', 10)`. [community]

224. **[community] Provider verification tests that use `stateHandlers` defined as plain synchronous functions (not returning a Promise) will silently skip database operations if the underlying ORM or data access layer is async — the state handler returns before the async operation completes, and Pact proceeds to send the verification request against an unseeded database.** This is because Pact's state handler invocation mechanism `await`s the return value of each handler — if the handler is `async`, awaiting it waits for the async operation; if the handler is synchronous but calls an async function without `return`, the async operation is fire-and-forget. The test runner does not throw an error because the state handler returns `undefined` which Pact treats as success. **Why it matters:** provider verification passes green because the route handler returns a valid response shape even with empty database state (e.g., returning an empty array for a list endpoint), but the response content is not what the consumer expected — causing production defects that the contract tests were supposed to prevent. **Fix:** all state handlers must be declared `async` and must `await` (or `return`) every database operation; use TypeScript's `Promise<void>` return type annotation to force the compiler to warn when an `async` function body has unawaited calls. [community]

225. **[community] When a consumer publishes a pact with a branch name containing a forward slash (e.g., `feature/PROJ-123-new-api`) to the Pact Broker, the broker stores the branch correctly but some CI systems that interpolate `${pactbroker.consumerVersionBranch}` into webhook URLs construct a malformed URL because the slash is not percent-encoded — causing the webhook to call `https://ci.example.com/trigger/feature/PROJ-123-new-api` instead of a properly encoded URL.** The Pact Broker's webhook template engine does not URL-encode substituted values, so branch names with path-unsafe characters will silently generate incorrectly formatted webhook trigger URLs. The downstream CI system interprets the extra path segments as a different route and returns a 404, causing the webhook to be marked as failed in the Broker's webhook delivery log — but since webhook failures are non-blocking by default, the provider verification pipeline is never triggered and the team does not notice until a pact regression reaches production. **Why it matters:** the failure mode is completely silent — the Broker UI shows webhook delivery failures but no alert is sent, and the provider is never notified that a new pact requires verification. **Fix:** normalize branch names to use hyphens instead of slashes at pact publish time (`GIT_BRANCH=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD | tr '/' '-')`); as a defensive measure, validate webhook delivery success in the Broker's delivery log as part of the consumer pipeline rather than treating webhook failures as silent background events. [community]

226. **[community] Pact verification suites that use `filterConsumerNames` to limit which consumers are verified in a given CI run will silently skip publishing verification results for the filtered-out consumers — the Broker records no result for those consumers under the current provider version, causing `can-i-deploy` to return "unknown" and block deployments for consumers that were not included in the filter.** `filterConsumerNames` is designed for targeted debugging and local development, not for production CI pipelines. When used in CI to speed up the verification run by only verifying a subset of consumers, the Broker interprets the absence of a verification result for the excluded consumers as "not yet verified" — equivalent to a pending state without the pending feature enabled. **Why it matters:** a pipeline that verifies only "ConsumerA" and "ConsumerB" but not "ConsumerC" will block ConsumerC from deploying forever, even if ConsumerC's pact content has not changed in months, because no verification result has ever been published for ConsumerC under the current provider SHA. **Fix:** never use `filterConsumerNames` in CI pipelines that publish results; if the full verification suite is too slow for CI, split it into multiple jobs that each verify a disjoint subset of consumers and all publish results — never skip publishing for any consumer. [community]

227. **[community] When a TypeScript consumer test uses `jest.mock()` to mock the HTTP client used by the production API adapter, the mocked client never actually calls the Pact mock server, meaning the consumer test passes but no pact file is generated — the test verifies the mock's behavior, not the real API client's contract.** This is the most common contract testing anti-pattern in TypeScript codebases: developers accustomed to unit testing with mocks apply the same pattern to Pact tests, replacing the real `fetch`/`axios` call with a Jest mock. The Pact mock server starts successfully, the interaction is registered, the "mocked" test passes, but `executeTest()` reports no interactions were received — in some configurations this silently generates an empty pact file rather than throwing. **Why it matters:** the team believes they have contract coverage for their API integration when in fact they have a test that verifies the mock's behavior and generates no pact file. The defect may go unnoticed for weeks if pact file publication to the Broker is not validated in CI. **Fix:** never mock the HTTP client in Pact consumer tests; the entire purpose of the test is to exercise the real client code against the Pact mock server. If the API adapter has complex initialization logic that requires mocking, refactor it to accept the base URL as a constructor parameter so the Pact mock server URL can be injected directly. [community]

## Cycle 43 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 311 — `constrainedArrayLike` for Min/Max Bounded Response Pagination Windows [official]

Paginated APIs typically return a bounded slice of results: the page size is always between 1 and the configured maximum (e.g., 1–50 items per page). Using `eachLike` for these responses creates an interaction that only requires the array to have at least one element with no upper bound — a provider returning 10,000 items in a single page would pass the pact. `constrainedArrayLike(template, min, max)` enforces both bounds simultaneously, generating an example array with `min` items. This is the correct matcher whenever the consumer renders a bounded window of results and its rendering logic has assumptions about the maximum number of items (e.g., a fixed-height list that clips at 10 rows).

**Tradeoff:** `constrainedArrayLike` generates exactly `min` example items in the pact file by default, which may not exercise multi-item rendering code in the consumer test. Pass an explicit `count` argument (the fourth parameter) to generate a larger representative array for richer consumer-side assertions, while still enforcing the min/max bounds during provider verification. If the `max` bound is business-logic-driven (e.g., controlled by a feature flag on the provider), avoid hardcoding it in the pact — use `atLeastLike(min)` instead and validate the max via a dedicated contract interaction that asserts the provider returns a 400 or truncates when the consumer requests more than the allowed maximum. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/product-search.pact.spec.ts
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { constrainedArrayLike, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'ProductCatalogUI',
  provider: 'ProductSearchService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('ProductSearchService GET /products?q=widget — page size boundaries', () => {
  it('returns 1–20 product items for a search result page', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('products matching "widget" exist in the catalog')
      .uponReceiving('GET /products?q=widget&page=1&pageSize=20 — bounded search results')
      .withRequest('GET', '/products', (builder) => {
        builder.query({ q: 'widget', page: '1', pageSize: '20' });
      })
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          // min=1, max=20, count=3 — generate 3 items for richer assertions
          items: constrainedArrayLike(
            { id: string('prod-001'), name: string('Widget Pro'), price: integer(1999) },
            1,   // minimum 1 item per page
            20,  // maximum 20 items per page (page size cap)
            3,   // generate 3 example items for consumer test assertions
          ),
          total: integer(47),
          page: integer(1),
          pageSize: integer(20),
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(
          `${mockServer.url}/products?q=widget&page=1&pageSize=20`,
        );
        const body = await res.json() as { items: unknown[]; total: number };
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        expect(body.items.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
        expect(body.items.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(20);
        expect(typeof body.total).toBe('number');
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 312 — `eachKeyMatches` + `eachValueMatches` for Dynamic Map Responses [official]

Some API endpoints return JSON objects whose keys are dynamic (e.g., locale codes, feature flag names, user-configurable field names) rather than a fixed schema. For these responses, `eachKeyMatches(rules)` validates that every key satisfies a regex pattern while ignoring the values, and `eachValueMatches(template)` validates that every value matches a type/format while ignoring the keys. Used together — with `eachKeyMatches` constraining the key pattern and `eachValueMatches` constraining the value type — these matchers express the full contract for a dictionary-shaped response without enumerating every possible key. This eliminates the need to create a separate interaction for every locale or feature flag the consumer might encounter.

**Tradeoff:** `eachKeyMatches` and `eachValueMatches` are V3/V4-only matchers and have no equivalent in Pact specification V2. If any consumers or providers in your ecosystem still use V2-generated pact files (e.g., via pact-ruby or older Go implementations), the verifier will reject the unrecognised matching rule and report a spec version incompatibility error. Confirm that all participants in the pact ecosystem are running V3 or higher before adopting these matchers. Additionally, these matchers cannot simultaneously constrain both keys and values in the same object node — compose them by nesting the `eachValueMatches` matcher as a child of a `like()` wrapper rather than applying both at the same object level. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/feature-flags.pact.spec.ts
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { eachKeyMatches, eachValueMatches, boolean, regex } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'FeatureFlagSDK',
  provider: 'FeatureFlagService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('FeatureFlagService GET /flags — dynamic key-value map response', () => {
  it('returns a map of flag names to boolean values', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('feature flags are configured for tenant acme')
      .uponReceiving('GET /flags for tenant acme — dynamic map of flag-name to bool')
      .withRequest('GET', '/flags', (builder) => {
        builder.headers({ 'X-Tenant-ID': 'acme' });
      })
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody(
          // Keys must match snake_case flag name pattern; values must be boolean
          eachKeyMatches(
            { 'new_checkout_flow': boolean(true) },
            [regex('[a-z][a-z0-9_]*', 'new_checkout_flow')],
          ),
        );
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/flags`, {
          headers: { 'X-Tenant-ID': 'acme' },
        });
        const flags = await res.json() as Record<string, boolean>;
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(flags)) {
          expect(typeof key).toBe('string');
          expect(typeof value).toBe('boolean');
        }
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 313 — `addGraphQLInteraction()` for Typed GraphQL Query Contracts [official]

Pact V4's `addGraphQLInteraction()` builder abstracts the GraphQL-over-HTTP transport details — it constructs the correct `application/json` POST body with `query`, `operationName`, and `variables` fields, so consumer tests express intent at the GraphQL operation level rather than at the raw HTTP level. Consumer tests call `withOperation('GetOrderDetails')`, `withVariables({ orderId: '123' })`, and `withQuery(gql\`...\`)`, while the provider verification points the `Verifier` at the running GraphQL server with no GraphQL-specific config needed — the verifier sends the serialized HTTP POST and validates the response body. This makes pact files generated from GraphQL tests readable by non-GraphQL tooling and portable across provider implementations.

**Tradeoff:** The `addGraphQLInteraction()` builder only supports `query` and `mutation` operation types; GraphQL `subscription` operations (which use WebSocket or SSE transport) cannot be expressed through this builder and require the Pact Plugins architecture with a custom transport plugin. Additionally, because the pact file records the raw GraphQL query string, schema evolution that renames a field but keeps the field alias in the query will generate a new pact interaction (the query string changed) even though the consumer code and the provider response shape are identical. Use query fragments stored in shared constants to prevent query string drift between test and production code from creating spurious pact diffs. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/order-gql.pact.spec.ts
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { string, integer, iso8601DateTime } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'OrderDashboardUI',
  provider: 'OrderGraphQLService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

const GET_ORDER_QUERY = `
  query GetOrderDetails($orderId: ID!) {
    order(id: $orderId) {
      id
      status
      createdAt
      lineItems { sku quantity unitPrice }
    }
  }
`;

describe('OrderGraphQLService — GetOrderDetails query contract', () => {
  it('returns structured order data for a valid orderId', async () => {
    await pact
      .addGraphQLInteraction()
      .given('order ord-999 exists with two line items')
      .uponReceiving('GetOrderDetails query for order ord-999')
      .withOperation('GetOrderDetails')
      .withVariables({ orderId: 'ord-999' })
      .withQuery(GET_ORDER_QUERY)
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          data: {
            order: {
              id: string('ord-999'),
              status: string('PROCESSING'),
              createdAt: iso8601DateTime(),
              lineItems: [
                { sku: string('SKU-A'), quantity: integer(2), unitPrice: integer(1500) },
              ],
            },
          },
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/graphql`, {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify({
            operationName: 'GetOrderDetails',
            query: GET_ORDER_QUERY,
            variables: { orderId: 'ord-999' },
          }),
        });
        const body = await res.json() as { data: { order: { status: string } } };
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        expect(body.data.order.status).toBeDefined();
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 314 — `expand-and-contract` Migration with Pact `fallbackBranch` Selector [official]

The expand-and-contract pattern for zero-downtime API field migrations proceeds in three phases: (1) provider adds a new field alongside the old one, (2) consumers migrate to the new field, (3) provider removes the old field. During phase 1, the consumer's main-branch pact still references the old field, so the provider's verification must pass against both the main-branch pact (old field only) and the consumer's migration-branch pact (both old and new fields). The `fallbackBranch` consumer version selector enables this by specifying a fallback branch name to use when no pact exists on `matchingBranch` — the provider verifies whichever branch is most current for each consumer. This eliminates the need to coordinate deployment windows between teams during the migration.

**Tradeoff:** `fallbackBranch` is a Pact Broker concept and requires the Broker to be running version 2.86.0 or later (the feature was added in that release). Teams using self-hosted Pact Broker instances that lag behind on upgrades will encounter an "unknown selector property" error in the verifier. A simpler (though less ergonomic) alternative is to use two explicit `{ branch: 'main' }` and `{ branch: 'feature/migrate-to-v2-api' }` selectors during the migration window and remove the feature branch selector after the consumer's migration branch is merged — this works on all Broker versions but requires manual selector cleanup. [official]

```typescript
// provider/verifier-config.ts — expand-and-contract with fallbackBranch selector
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

async function runProviderVerification() {
  const verifier = new VerifierV3({
    provider: 'PaymentService',
    providerBaseUrl: `http://localhost:${process.env.PROVIDER_PORT ?? 3001}`,
    pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
    pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
    consumerVersionSelectors: [
      // Phase 1: verify consumers on main branch AND any matching migration branches
      { mainBranch: true },
      {
        matchingBranch: true,
        // During expand phase, fall back to main if no matching consumer branch exists
        fallbackBranch: 'main',
      },
      // Always verify whatever is deployed to production
      { deployedOrReleased: true },
    ],
    enablePending: true,
    publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
    providerVersion: process.env.GIT_SHA!,
    providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
    stateHandlers: {
      'payment method card-tok-123 exists for customer cust-456': async () => {
        // Seed both old `cardToken` and new `paymentMethodId` fields
        await seedPaymentMethod({
          cardToken: 'card-tok-123',        // legacy field (phase 1: keep)
          paymentMethodId: 'pm-xyz-789',    // new field (phase 1: add)
          customerId: 'cust-456',
        });
      },
    },
  });

  await verifier.verifyProvider();
}

runProviderVerification().catch((err) => {
  console.error('Provider verification failed:', err);
  process.exit(1);
});
```

### Pattern 315 — Asynchronous Message Contract with `addAsynchronousInteraction` and SNS/SQS Body Envelope [official]

Event-driven services that publish to AWS SNS or SQS wrap the domain event in a transport envelope: `{ "Type": "Notification", "Message": "<JSON-escaped-string>", "MessageAttributes": {...} }`. Consumer Pact tests for these services must model the full envelope so that provider verification sends a matching envelope to the consumer's message handler — not just the raw domain event. Using `addAsynchronousInteraction()` with the envelope shape as the `withContent()` body, and `MatchersV3.string()` for the escaped inner `Message` field, captures this two-layer structure in the pact. The consumer's message handler under test must deserialize both the outer envelope and the inner JSON string, so the test exercises the complete deserialization path.

**Tradeoff:** Encoding the inner domain event as a JSON-escaped string inside the `Message` field means the pact file contains a string value for `Message` rather than a structured object — the Pact Broker's UI renders this as an opaque string and the inner event schema is not diffable in the broker's change-detection logic. Teams that want diffable inner event schemas should unwrap the SNS envelope before writing the pact (model only the inner domain event) and use a separate integration test to validate the envelope structure. This trades pact accuracy for readability and diff visibility. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/order-shipped-handler.pact.spec.ts
import { MessageConsumerPact, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { string, iso8601DateTime, uuid } = MatchersV3;

const messagePact = new MessageConsumerPact({
  consumer: 'ShipmentNotificationService',
  provider: 'OrderFulfillmentService',
  dir: 'pacts',
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('OrderFulfillmentService — OrderShipped SNS message contract', () => {
  it('handles the full SNS envelope containing an OrderShipped domain event', async () => {
    await messagePact
      .given('order ord-222 has been shipped')
      .expectsToReceive('SNS notification envelope for OrderShipped event')
      .withContent({
        // Model the full SNS envelope — consumer code deserializes both layers
        Type: string('Notification'),
        MessageId: uuid(),
        TopicArn: string('arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:order-events'),
        Message: string(
          // Example of the JSON-escaped inner domain event
          JSON.stringify({
            eventType: 'OrderShipped',
            orderId: 'ord-222',
            shippedAt: '2026-05-14T10:00:00Z',
            trackingNumber: 'TRK-ABC-123',
          }),
        ),
        Timestamp: iso8601DateTime(),
      })
      .withMetadata({ 'content-type': 'application/json' })
      .verify(async (message: Record<string, unknown>) => {
        // Consumer handler: deserialize envelope, then inner event
        const envelope = message as { Type: string; Message: string };
        expect(envelope.Type).toBe('Notification');
        const innerEvent = JSON.parse(envelope.Message) as {
          eventType: string;
          orderId: string;
          trackingNumber: string;
        };
        expect(innerEvent.eventType).toBe('OrderShipped');
        expect(typeof innerEvent.trackingNumber).toBe('string');
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 316 — `InterfaceToTemplate<T>` Utility for Type-Safe Pact Body Builders [official]

TypeScript consumer tests that construct pact body objects using `MatchersV3` functions run into a type mismatch: the API interface declares `{ price: number }` but the body builder must contain `{ price: ReturnType<typeof integer> }` — passing the raw interface type produces a TypeScript compiler error. Pact-js exports an `InterfaceToTemplate<T>` utility type that transforms every `T[K]` leaf type into `T[K] | Matcher<T[K]>`, meaning the body builder object can contain either a raw value or a matcher for each field, satisfying the compiler without using `as any` casts. This pattern enforces that the body builder shape exactly matches the interface at compile time — if the interface adds a required field, the TypeScript compiler will report an error at the pact test's `jsonBody()` call site.

**Tradeoff:** `InterfaceToTemplate<T>` is a deep-recursive mapped type. For interfaces with more than 5–6 levels of nesting (e.g., complex order objects with nested address, payment, and line item sub-types), TypeScript's type instantiation depth limit may be exceeded, causing "Type instantiation is excessively deep" compiler errors. In practice, most API response interfaces are shallow enough for this not to be an issue. If the depth limit is hit, split the deeply nested type into named sub-types and apply `InterfaceToTemplate` at each sub-type independently rather than at the root type. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/invoice.pact.spec.ts
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3, InterfaceToTemplate } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { string, integer, decimal, iso8601Date, uuid } = MatchersV3;

// The production API interface — shared with the provider via an SDK package
interface Invoice {
  invoiceId: string;
  customerId: string;
  issuedDate: string;    // ISO 8601 date
  totalAmountCents: number;
  taxAmountCents: number;
  lineItemCount: number;
}

// InterfaceToTemplate makes every field accept either a raw value or a Pact matcher
type InvoiceTemplate = InterfaceToTemplate<Invoice>;

const invoiceBody: InvoiceTemplate = {
  invoiceId: uuid(),
  customerId: string('cust-abc'),
  issuedDate: iso8601Date(),
  totalAmountCents: integer(15000),
  taxAmountCents: integer(1500),
  lineItemCount: integer(3),
};

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'BillingPortalUI',
  provider: 'InvoiceService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('InvoiceService GET /invoices/:id — type-safe body builder', () => {
  it('returns a well-typed Invoice object', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('invoice inv-001 exists')
      .uponReceiving('GET /invoices/inv-001 — type-safe invoice body')
      .withRequest('GET', '/invoices/inv-001')
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        // invoiceBody is type-checked against InvoiceTemplate — compiler error if fields are missing
        builder.jsonBody(invoiceBody);
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/invoices/inv-001`);
        const body = await res.json() as Invoice;
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        expect(typeof body.invoiceId).toBe('string');
        expect(typeof body.totalAmountCents).toBe('number');
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 317 — `requestFilter` Middleware for Short-Lived JWKS-Signed Token Injection [official]

Provider verification suites that run against APIs protected by short-lived JWTs signed with a JWKS endpoint face a bootstrapping problem: the token generated during test suite startup may expire mid-run for long verification suites (50+ interactions). Using `requestFilter` as an Express middleware that inspects each outbound verification request and injects a freshly generated token per-interaction (or per-batch via a token cache with a 50-second TTL) solves expiry mid-run without requiring test parallelism changes. The `requestFilter` receives the outbound `IncomingMessage` and has access to `request.headers` before each verification HTTP call — overwriting `Authorization` in the filter ensures every interaction gets a valid token regardless of run duration.

**Tradeoff:** `requestFilter` adds real network latency to the provider token endpoint for every interaction. For suites with hundreds of interactions, this per-interaction token fetch can add 30–60 seconds to the total verification runtime. Mitigate by caching the token with a TTL set to `expiresIn - 30s` (a 30-second safety margin before actual expiry) so that the token is refreshed at most once per TTL window rather than once per interaction. If the token endpoint is itself protected or rate-limited, use a mock token endpoint in CI that returns a valid test JWT without calling real auth infrastructure. [official]

```typescript
// provider/verification-token-filter.ts
import { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from 'http';
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

interface TokenCache {
  token: string;
  expiresAt: number; // epoch ms
}

let tokenCache: TokenCache | null = null;

async function getVerificationToken(): Promise<string> {
  const now = Date.now();
  // Cache hit: reuse if more than 30 seconds remain before expiry
  if (tokenCache && tokenCache.expiresAt - now > 30_000) {
    return tokenCache.token;
  }
  // Fetch a new token from the OIDC client credentials endpoint
  const res = await fetch(process.env.TOKEN_ENDPOINT!, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
    body: new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: 'client_credentials',
      client_id: process.env.CLIENT_ID!,
      client_secret: process.env.CLIENT_SECRET!,
      scope: 'api:verify',
    }),
  });
  const data = await res.json() as { access_token: string; expires_in: number };
  tokenCache = {
    token: data.access_token,
    expiresAt: now + data.expires_in * 1000,
  };
  return tokenCache.token;
}

const verifier = new VerifierV3({
  provider: 'ProtectedResourceService',
  providerBaseUrl: `http://localhost:${process.env.PROVIDER_PORT ?? 4000}`,
  pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
  pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
  consumerVersionSelectors: [{ mainBranch: true }, { deployedOrReleased: true }],
  publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
  providerVersion: process.env.GIT_SHA!,
  providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
  // Inject a fresh (or cached) token before every verification request
  requestFilter: (
    req: IncomingMessage,
    _res: ServerResponse,
    next: () => void,
  ) => {
    getVerificationToken()
      .then((token) => {
        req.headers['authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`;
        next();
      })
      .catch((err) => {
        console.error('Token fetch failed during verification:', err);
        next(); // proceed without auth — interaction will fail with 401 as expected
      });
  },
});

verifier.verifyProvider().catch((err) => {
  console.error('Verification failed:', err);
  process.exit(1);
});
```

---

### Pattern 318 — Provider State Parameter Passing via `given(state, params)` Overload [official]

Provider states often need to be parameterized: the state "product X has Y units in stock" applies to any product and any quantity, not just one hardcoded product ID. Pact V4 supports a two-argument `given(stateName, params)` overload that serializes the `params` object into the provider state request body. On the provider side, the `stateHandlers` key is the state name string, and the handler receives the deserialized `params` as its argument. This eliminates the combinatorial explosion of provider state strings like `"product abc-123 has 5 units in stock"`, `"product xyz-456 has 0 units in stock"` — replacing them with a single parameterized state `"product has N units in stock"` with `{ productId, quantity }` params.

**Tradeoff:** Parameterized provider states require all participants to run Pact specification V3 or higher. V2 does not support state parameters — the params object is silently dropped and the state handler receives an empty argument. If you have a mixed ecosystem with some V2 consumers that share a provider, the provider's `stateHandlers` must handle both the parameterized V3 call and the unparameterized V2 call for the same logical state — typically by defaulting to a sentinel value when `params` is empty. Always log the received params at the start of each state handler to make this distinction debuggable in CI output. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/inventory.pact.spec.ts — parameterized provider state
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { string, integer, fromProviderState } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'InventoryCheckWidget',
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('InventoryService GET /inventory/:productId — parameterized state', () => {
  it('returns stock level for a product with known quantity', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      // Pass productId and quantity as state params — single reusable state name
      .given('product has N units in stock', { productId: 'prod-widgets', quantity: 42 })
      .uponReceiving('GET /inventory/prod-widgets — check stock level')
      .withRequest('GET', '/inventory/prod-widgets')
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          productId: string('prod-widgets'),
          quantityAvailable: integer(42),
          warehouseLocation: string('WAREHOUSE-A'),
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/inventory/prod-widgets`);
        const body = await res.json() as { quantityAvailable: number };
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        expect(body.quantityAvailable).toBe(42);
      });
  });

  it('returns zero stock for an out-of-stock product', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('product has N units in stock', { productId: 'prod-discontinued', quantity: 0 })
      .uponReceiving('GET /inventory/prod-discontinued — out of stock')
      .withRequest('GET', '/inventory/prod-discontinued')
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          productId: string('prod-discontinued'),
          quantityAvailable: integer(0),
          warehouseLocation: string('N/A'),
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/inventory/prod-discontinued`);
        const body = await res.json() as { quantityAvailable: number };
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        expect(body.quantityAvailable).toBe(0);
      });
  });
});

// provider/state-handlers.ts — single handler receiving params
export const stateHandlers = {
  'product has N units in stock': async (params: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    const productId = (params['productId'] as string) ?? 'default-prod';
    const quantity  = (params['quantity']  as number) ?? 1;
    console.log(`[state] seeding product ${productId} with ${quantity} units`);
    await db.upsertProduct({ id: productId, quantityAvailable: quantity });
  },
};
```

### Pattern 319 — Bi-Directional Contract Testing (BDCT) with OpenAPI Schema Upload [official]

Bi-directional contract testing (BDCT) inverts the verification flow for providers that already publish an OpenAPI schema: the provider uploads its schema to PactFlow and the platform performs schema-vs-consumer-pact compatibility checks automatically — no provider verification test code is needed. The consumer still writes standard Pact consumer tests that generate a pact file. PactFlow then compares the consumer's pact interactions against the provider's OpenAPI schema, flagging any interaction that uses a field not declared in the schema or requires a request structure the schema does not allow. This is particularly valuable for third-party or public APIs where running a provider verification suite is not feasible.

**Tradeoff:** BDCT is a PactFlow-specific feature and does not work with the open-source Pact Broker. Teams running self-hosted Pact Broker cannot use BDCT and must implement traditional provider verification. Additionally, BDCT's schema comparison is only as accurate as the OpenAPI schema — providers with incomplete or overly permissive schemas (e.g., `additionalProperties: true` on every object) will produce false-positive compatibility results, creating a false sense of safety. Before adopting BDCT, validate that the provider's OpenAPI schema is generated from code (not hand-written) and enforced via a linting rule that rejects `additionalProperties: true`. [official]

```typescript
// scripts/publish-provider-schema.ts — upload OpenAPI schema for BDCT
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import path from 'path';

const SCHEMA_PATH  = path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'openapi.yaml');
const PROVIDER     = process.env.PROVIDER_NAME!;
const VERSION      = process.env.GIT_SHA!;
const BRANCH       = process.env.GIT_BRANCH!;
const BROKER_URL   = process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!;
const BROKER_TOKEN = process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!;

// PactFlow CLI: publish the provider's OpenAPI schema for BDCT
const publishCmd = [
  'pactflow publish-provider-contract',
  `"${SCHEMA_PATH}"`,
  `--provider "${PROVIDER}"`,
  `--provider-app-version "${VERSION}"`,
  `--branch "${BRANCH}"`,
  '--content-type "application/yaml"',
  '--verification-success',
  `--broker-base-url "${BROKER_URL}"`,
  `--broker-token "${BROKER_TOKEN}"`,
].join(' ');

try {
  const output = execSync(publishCmd, { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'] });
  console.log('Provider schema published for BDCT:\n', output);
} catch (err: unknown) {
  console.error('Schema publish failed:', (err as { stdout?: string }).stdout ?? err);
  process.exit(1);
}
```

---

### Pattern 320 — `afterEach` Teardown Guard for Leaked Mock Server Handles [community]

When Pact consumer tests fail inside `executeTest()` before the mock server's response is consumed, the mock server socket may remain open and keep the Jest process alive after the test run completes — causing Jest to hang with the "A worker process has failed to exit gracefully" warning. Adding a Jest `afterEach` hook that calls `pact.cleanup()` (or the equivalent `mockServer.stop()` for manually managed servers) ensures the mock server is torn down even when the test throws. Without this guard, a single test failure can cause the entire Jest run to hang indefinitely in CI, consuming runner minutes and blocking the pipeline for all subsequent commits.

**Tradeoff:** `pact.cleanup()` is idempotent for successfully-completed `executeTest()` calls — calling it in `afterEach` after a successful test is a no-op and safe. However, calling `cleanup()` inside a `afterAll` block rather than `afterEach` means a single test failure early in the suite will leave the mock server running for all subsequent tests in the same `describe` block — those subsequent tests will receive unexpected responses from the still-running prior-test mock server. Always use `afterEach`, not `afterAll`, for cleanup when multiple interactions are registered across separate `it()` blocks sharing the same `PactV4` instance. [community]

```typescript
// consumer/resilient-pact-test.ts — afterEach cleanup guard
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { string } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'NotificationService',
  provider: 'TemplateService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

// Guard: tear down mock server after every test, success or failure
afterEach(async () => {
  try {
    // cleanup() is safe to call even if executeTest() already cleaned up
    // It ensures the mock server socket is released regardless of test outcome
    await (pact as unknown as { cleanup?: () => Promise<void> }).cleanup?.();
  } catch {
    // Swallow cleanup errors — the important thing is releasing the socket handle
  }
});

describe('TemplateService GET /templates/:id — teardown guard', () => {
  it('returns a template for a known template ID', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('template tmpl-001 exists')
      .uponReceiving('GET /templates/tmpl-001')
      .withRequest('GET', '/templates/tmpl-001')
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          id: string('tmpl-001'),
          name: string('Welcome Email'),
          subject: string('Welcome to Acme!'),
          bodyHtml: string('<h1>Welcome</h1>'),
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/templates/tmpl-001`);
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        const body = await res.json() as { name: string };
        expect(typeof body.name).toBe('string');
        // Simulate a test failure mid-interaction to validate cleanup guard
        // throw new Error('Simulated failure — mock server must still close');
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 321 — `{ deployed: 'production', consumer: 'MobileApp' }` Scoped Selector for Multi-Consumer Verification [official]

In ecosystems with many consumers, verifying all deployed-to-production pacts on every provider CI run is expensive and can make the verification suite slow. For providers that serve a mix of web and mobile consumers, mobile app versions are released (and thus remain deployed-to-production for longer) while web consumers deploy frequently. Scoping the `deployedOrReleased` selector to specific consumers via the `consumer` property allows the provider to run targeted verification: mobile consumers get an explicit `{ deployed: 'production', consumer: 'MobileApp' }` selector (which verifies exactly the production-deployed version), while web consumers use `{ matchingBranch: true }` for fast-path PR verification. This reduces average verification suite runtime without sacrificing safety for high-stakes deployed versions.

**Tradeoff:** Consumer-scoped selectors require the team to maintain the selector list as consumers are onboarded and offboarded. A new mobile consumer that joins the ecosystem will not be included in production verification until its selector is added to the provider's verifier config. Mitigate by using the unscoped `{ deployedOrReleased: true }` selector as a catch-all "safety net" alongside the scoped selectors — the catch-all picks up any consumer not explicitly named, while the scoped selectors enable per-consumer environment granularity. Remove the catch-all only after all consumers have been explicitly enumerated and the team has a process for updating the selector list on consumer onboarding. [official]

```typescript
// provider/verifier-multi-consumer.ts — scoped selectors for mixed consumer types
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const verifier = new VerifierV3({
  provider: 'UserProfileService',
  providerBaseUrl: `http://localhost:${process.env.PROVIDER_PORT ?? 5000}`,
  pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
  pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
  consumerVersionSelectors: [
    // Web consumers: verify PR branches + main
    { mainBranch: true },
    { matchingBranch: true },
    // Mobile consumers: only the specific production-deployed version (they stay deployed longer)
    { deployed: 'production', consumer: 'IOSApp' },
    { deployed: 'production', consumer: 'AndroidApp' },
    // Released versions (mobile app store versions) — kept for historical compatibility
    { released: true, consumer: 'IOSApp' },
    { released: true, consumer: 'AndroidApp' },
    // Catch-all: any newly onboarded consumer not yet enumerated above
    { deployedOrReleased: true },
  ],
  enablePending: true,
  publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
  providerVersion: process.env.GIT_SHA!,
  providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
});

verifier.verifyProvider()
  .then(() => console.log('All consumer contracts verified.'))
  .catch((err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });
```

### Pattern 322 — `pact-broker record-deployment` and `record-release` CLI Commands for Environment Tracking [official]

The Pact Broker's `can-i-deploy` check uses environment-aware deployment records to answer "is version X safe to deploy to environment Y?" These records are created by `pact-broker record-deployment` (for services deployed to a single instance per environment, e.g., Kubernetes deployments) and `pact-broker record-release` (for artifacts published to a package registry that multiple environments consume simultaneously, e.g., mobile apps or npm packages). Failing to call `record-deployment` after a successful deploy means `can-i-deploy --to-environment production` will never find a recorded deployment for the service and will always report "no deployment recorded" — which either blocks all subsequent deployments (if `--ignore-no-pacts` is not set) or silently allows deployments without any pact check (if `--ignore-no-pacts` is set). Both outcomes undermine the contract testing safety net.

**Tradeoff:** `record-deployment` marks only one version as deployed per environment per application — calling it for a new version automatically unmarks the previous version in that environment. This is correct behavior for rolling/canary deployments where only one version is active at a time. For blue-green deployments where two versions are simultaneously live, the Broker's single-deployment-per-environment model is incorrect: recording the "green" version as deployed will unmark the "blue" version, making `can-i-deploy` believe the blue version is no longer in production when both are serving traffic. Use `--application-instance` flag to differentiate the blue and green slot names (`record-deployment --application-instance blue`) so the Broker tracks both concurrently. [official]

```bash
# deploy-pipeline.sh — record deployment after successful Kubernetes rollout

set -euo pipefail

SERVICE="${SERVICE_NAME:?SERVICE_NAME must be set}"
VERSION="${GIT_SHA:?GIT_SHA must be set}"
ENVIRONMENT="${DEPLOY_ENVIRONMENT:?DEPLOY_ENVIRONMENT must be set}"

# Step 1: verify pact compatibility before deploying
npx pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant "${SERVICE}" \
  --version "${VERSION}" \
  --to-environment "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --broker-base-url "${PACT_BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token "${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}" \
  --retry-while-unknown 30 \
  --retry-interval 10

# Step 2: perform the actual deployment (e.g., kubectl rollout)
kubectl set image "deployment/${SERVICE}" "${SERVICE}=${IMAGE}:${VERSION}"
kubectl rollout status "deployment/${SERVICE}" --timeout=300s

# Step 3: record the deployment AFTER successful rollout
# This makes can-i-deploy aware that this version is now live in the environment
npx pact-broker record-deployment \
  --pacticipant "${SERVICE}" \
  --version "${VERSION}" \
  --environment "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --broker-base-url "${PACT_BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token "${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}"

echo "Deployment of ${SERVICE}@${VERSION} to ${ENVIRONMENT} recorded in Pact Broker."
```

### Pattern 323 — `withComment()` on Error Interactions for Failure-Mode Contract Documentation [official]

Pact V4's `withComment()` builder method attaches a free-text annotation to an interaction that is rendered in the Pact Broker UI and included in verification failure reports. For interactions that model error conditions (400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 503 Service Unavailable), `withComment()` provides essential context about why the consumer cares about this specific error shape — what field in the error response body the consumer displays to the user, or what retry/fallback logic the consumer triggers. Without this context, provider engineers seeing a failing error-response interaction have no way to know whether the error body structure is a contractual obligation or an incidental implementation detail.

**Tradeoff:** `withComment()` accepts only a string and does not support structured metadata (e.g., a link to the consumer feature ticket). Teams that want richer metadata on interactions should use `withTestName()` in conjunction with `withComment()` — `withTestName()` sets the Jest/Mocha test name that appears in broker reports (useful for linking to test IDs in external tracking systems) while `withComment()` carries the human-readable explanation. Comments are stored in the pact file but are not used by the Pact matching engine — they have zero impact on verification pass/fail outcomes and can be updated freely without triggering a new pact hash. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/checkout-errors.pact.spec.ts — documented error interactions
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'CheckoutUI',
  provider: 'PaymentService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('PaymentService POST /payments — error response contracts', () => {
  it('receives a structured 422 when the card is declined', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('payment card card-tok-expired is expired')
      .uponReceiving('POST /payments — expired card decline 422')
      // Document WHY the consumer needs this specific error shape
      .withComment(
        'CheckoutUI renders body.error.code to select the correct user-facing ' +
        'error message (CARD_EXPIRED → "Your card has expired, please update your payment method"). ' +
        'body.error.declineCode is passed to the analytics event for funnel tracking.',
      )
      .withRequest('POST', '/payments', (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({ cardToken: string('card-tok-expired'), amount: integer(5000) });
      })
      .willRespondWith(422, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          error: {
            code: string('CARD_EXPIRED'),
            declineCode: string('expired_card'),
            message: string('Your card has expired.'),
          },
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/payments`, {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify({ cardToken: 'card-tok-expired', amount: 5000 }),
        });
        const body = await res.json() as { error: { code: string; declineCode: string } };
        expect(res.status).toBe(422);
        expect(body.error.code).toBe('CARD_EXPIRED');
        expect(body.error.declineCode).toBe('expired_card');
      });
  });
});
```

### Pattern 324 — Shared Provider State Seeding Library with Transaction Rollback [community]

Large provider verification suites accumulate dozens of `stateHandlers`, each seeding slightly different data configurations. Without coordination, state handlers leave residual data in the test database that can bleed into subsequent interactions — an order seeded in one state handler may appear in a list-all-orders response tested in a later interaction, inflating the array length and causing matcher failures. Wrapping every state handler in a database transaction that is rolled back after the interaction (via the teardown `action: 'teardown'` lifecycle) ensures perfect isolation between interactions without requiring full database truncation between each test. A shared `withTransactionalState(name, setup)` helper function enforces this pattern across all state handlers.

**Tradeoff:** Database transaction rollback only works for databases that support ACID transactions (PostgreSQL, MySQL with InnoDB). State handlers that interact with external systems (Redis cache invalidation, Elasticsearch index updates, S3 file uploads) cannot be rolled back transactionally — these side effects must be cleaned up explicitly in the teardown handler. If the provider mixes database state with external system side effects in the same state, consider splitting the state handler into two: one that sets up transactional state and one that manages external side effects, both registered under the same state name via a shared `stateHandlerExtensions` pattern. [community]

```typescript
// provider/test-support/transactional-state.ts
import { db } from '../database'; // your ORM/Knex instance

type SetupFn = (params: Record<string, unknown>) => Promise<void>;

/**
 * Wraps a state handler in a database transaction that rolls back after the interaction.
 * Prevents state bleed between Pact interactions in the same verification run.
 */
export function withTransactionalState(
  name: string,
  setup: SetupFn,
): Record<string, (params: Record<string, unknown>, action?: string) => Promise<void>> {
  let trx: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof db.transaction>> | null = null;

  return {
    [name]: async (params: Record<string, unknown>, action?: string) => {
      if (action === 'teardown') {
        // Rollback on teardown — undo all database mutations from setup
        if (trx) {
          await trx.rollback();
          trx = null;
          console.log(`[state:teardown] rolled back transaction for "${name}"`);
        }
        return;
      }
      // Setup: begin a transaction, run the seeding function within it
      trx = await db.transaction();
      try {
        await setup(params);
        // Do NOT commit — intentionally leave the transaction open until teardown
        console.log(`[state:setup] seeded "${name}" params=${JSON.stringify(params)}`);
      } catch (err) {
        await trx.rollback();
        trx = null;
        throw err;
      }
    },
  };
}

// Usage in provider/state-handlers.ts:
// export const stateHandlers = {
//   ...withTransactionalState('order ord-001 exists', async (params) => {
//     await db('orders').insert({ id: params.orderId ?? 'ord-001', status: 'ACTIVE' });
//   }),
// };
```

### Pattern 325 — `{ mainBranch: true }` Selector with `pacticipantVersionNumbers` Audit Log for Drift Detection [community]

When a provider CI run completes successfully against `{ mainBranch: true }` but then a consumer deploys a pact-breaking change to its main branch within the same sprint, the provider's next CI run may fail with a contract violation that is genuinely unexpected. Capturing the exact `pacticipantVersionNumbers` from each completed verification run (available in the Pact Broker's `/pacts/provider/:provider/latest` API response) and persisting them as a structured JSON artifact in CI allows teams to diff the consumer pact versions verified in run N versus run N-1. When a verification failure appears in run N, comparing the artifact shows exactly which consumer version changed between the two runs — narrowing the investigation from "something broke the contract" to "ConsumerA version abc123 introduced the breaking change."

**Tradeoff:** Persisting the pacticipant versions artifact adds a Pact Broker API call to every provider CI run and requires storing the JSON artifact between pipeline runs (e.g., in CI artifact storage or an S3 bucket). If the CI system purges artifacts after a short retention window (e.g., 7 days), diffs between runs separated by more than 7 days will not be available. Extend the artifact retention to at least 30 days (or the sprint length + buffer) to ensure the audit log covers the full sprint window where contract regressions are most likely to appear. [community]

```typescript
// scripts/capture-pact-versions.ts — run after verification to log verified consumer versions
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

async function capturePacticipantVersions(): Promise<void> {
  const provider = process.env.PROVIDER_NAME!;
  const brokerUrl = process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!;
  const token     = process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!;
  const runId     = process.env.CI_RUN_ID ?? 'local';

  // Fetch the latest verification matrix from the Pact Broker HAL API
  const url = `${brokerUrl}/pacts/provider/${encodeURIComponent(provider)}/latest`;
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
      Accept: 'application/hal+json',
    },
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    console.warn(`Could not fetch pact versions: ${res.status} ${res.statusText}`);
    return;
  }

  const data = await res.json() as {
    _embedded?: { pacts?: Array<{ consumer: { name: string }; _links: { self: { name: string } } }> };
  };

  const snapshot = {
    capturedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    provider,
    runId,
    consumers: (data._embedded?.pacts ?? []).map((p) => ({
      consumer: p.consumer.name,
      pactVersion: p._links.self.name,
    })),
  };

  const outPath = path.resolve(process.cwd(), `pact-version-snapshot-${runId}.json`);
  writeFileSync(outPath, JSON.stringify(snapshot, null, 2));
  console.log(`Pact version snapshot written to ${outPath}`);
  console.table(snapshot.consumers);
}

capturePacticipantVersions().catch((err) => {
  console.error('Version capture failed (non-blocking):', err);
  // Non-blocking: don't exit(1) — capturing versions is an audit feature, not a gate
});
```

### Community Production Lessons — Cycle 43 [community]

228. **[community] When a consumer test uses `withRequest('GET', '/resource')` with no query parameter matchers and the production API adapter appends a `?_cache-bust=<timestamp>` query parameter to every request, the Pact mock server returns a 400 because the actual request URL does not match the interaction's expected URL — the mock server performs an exact match on the query string by default.** Pact's mock server applies strict matching on all request components that are specified in the interaction and ignores components that are not specified — but this rule applies to unspecified query parameters only if the interaction is defined with no `query` builder call at all. Once any query parameter is added via `.withRequest(...).query({...})`, the mock server switches to "all-specified-params must match exactly" mode and rejects extra parameters. The failure manifests as a mysterious 400 from the Pact mock server with a body of "Unexpected request" — not a clear message about the extra query parameter. **Why it matters:** the consumer code appears to be exercising the real API adapter, but the adapter's cache-busting logic was added later and the consumer test was never updated — the test was silently passing because the test environment injected the adapter differently than production. **Fix:** include `_cache-bust` (or any implementation-added query parameter) in the interaction's `withRequest` builder using a regex matcher: `.query({ '_cache-bust': regex('\\d+', '1715644800000') })` — this matches any numeric timestamp without hardcoding a specific value. [community]

229. **[community] Provider verification suites that declare `stateHandlers` as an object literal defined inside the `new VerifierV3({...})` constructor call will lose `this` context for class-based repositories — calling `this.userRepository.create(...)` inside a state handler arrow function throws "Cannot read property 'create' of undefined" if `userRepository` is a class instance property accessed via `this`.** Arrow functions capture the lexical `this` from the enclosing scope. When the `stateHandlers` object is defined as a property inside the `VerifierV3` constructor options object, the enclosing lexical scope is the module scope (not a class instance), so `this` is `undefined` in strict mode. Developers who refactor a state handler out of a test helper class and into an inline object literal unknowingly break `this` binding without any TypeScript compiler warning — the compiler sees `this` as the global object type, not `undefined`, in non-strict-mode files. **Why it matters:** the bug is environment-dependent: it manifests as a runtime crash in CI (strict mode) but may pass locally if the developer's TypeScript config does not enforce strict mode. **Fix:** define state handlers as named functions (not arrow functions) using `function` keyword syntax if `this` context is required, or inject repository instances into a closure before defining the handlers: `const repo = this.userRepository; stateHandlers: { 'user exists': async () => repo.create({...}) }`. [community]

230. **[community] When a Pact consumer test generates a pact file and the pact is published to the broker with `providerVersionBranch` set to a branch name that matches the consumer's Git branch, but the branch was created from a stale base (not rebased on main), the provider's `matchingBranch: true` selector will find and verify the pact — but the compatibility matrix will show the pact as unverified for the provider's main branch even after the consumer branch is merged.** This happens because `matchingBranch` matches the branch name, not the merge base. After the consumer branch merges to main, the consumer's main-branch pact (a new version published by the merge commit CI run) is a different pact version than the branch pact — the `matchingBranch` verification result applies to the branch pact version, not to the merged main pact version. The new main pact version will be verified by `mainBranch: true` on the provider's next CI run, but there is a window between the consumer merge and the provider's next CI run where `can-i-deploy` for the consumer's main branch shows "unverified." **Why it matters:** teams that require `can-i-deploy` to be green before merging to main see a catch-22: the consumer branch pact is verified, but the main pact is not yet verified, blocking deployment until the provider runs CI independently. **Fix:** trigger a provider CI run via a webhook `contract_published` event whenever the consumer publishes a new pact on its main branch — the `contract_requiring_verification_published` webhook payload includes the consumer name and version, enabling targeted provider verification. [community]

231. **[community] Consumer tests that use `PactV4.addInteraction().willRespondWith(statusCode, builder => builder.jsonBody({...}))` with a response status code of 204 (No Content) and then also call `builder.jsonBody({...})` will generate a pact file where the interaction specifies both `status: 204` and a non-empty response body — the provider verification step will then fail because the provider correctly returns a 204 with no body, which the Pact verifier rejects because the pact declares an expected body.** HTTP 204 No Content explicitly prohibits a response body. The Pact mock server in consumer tests is permissive about this — it will serve the declared body even for a 204 status, making the consumer test pass. But the provider verifier is strict: it checks the actual response body against the pact's declared body and fails when the actual 204 body is empty. **Why it matters:** the consumer test passes locally, the provider verifies successfully on a provider stub that incorrectly returns a body with 204, but the real provider follows the HTTP spec and returns 204 with no body — causing the verification to fail only in the integration environment. **Fix:** for 204 interactions, call `willRespondWith(204)` with no body builder callback, or use `willRespondWith(204, builder => { /* no body call */ })` — and validate consumer-side that the response handler does not attempt to call `response.json()` on a 204, which throws a JSON parse error. [community]

232. **[community] Teams that run `pact-broker can-i-deploy` as a blocking gate in their CD pipeline but do not set `--retry-while-unknown` will encounter intermittent deployment blocks when the provider's verification pipeline is slower than the consumer's and has not yet published a result for the consumer's new pact version — `can-i-deploy` returns "unknown" (exit code 0 in some broker versions, exit code 1 in others depending on `--to-environment` vs `--to` flag usage), and the differing exit codes between broker versions create inconsistent pipeline behavior across teams that upgraded their Pact CLI at different times.** The `can-i-deploy` exit code contract changed between Pact CLI versions: versions before 1.63.0 returned exit code 0 for "unknown" when using `--to-environment`, while versions 1.63.0+ return exit code 1 for "unknown" regardless of which flag is used. Teams that pinned their CLI version locally but upgraded in CI without checking release notes see failures in CI that cannot be reproduced locally. **Why it matters:** a pipeline that was green for months suddenly starts failing after a CI image base image update that upgraded `@pact-foundation/pact-cli` — the error message "Unknown result" is not actionable without knowing the exit code change. **Fix:** always pin `@pact-foundation/pact-cli` to an exact version in `package.json` (not `^` or `~` ranges) and include the CLI version in the CI pipeline's dependency lock file; use `--retry-while-unknown 30 --retry-interval 10` to handle the timing window where the provider has not yet published verification results. [community]

### Pattern 326 — `fromProviderState` Matcher for Auto-Generated IDs with Type Assertion [official]

When a provider auto-generates resource IDs (UUIDs, database sequences, snowflake IDs) and returns them in the response body, consumer tests that hardcode an example ID will fail provider verification whenever the auto-generation algorithm produces a different value. The `fromProviderState(expression, exampleValue)` matcher solves this by allowing the provider's state handler to return a value that is injected into the interaction at verification time — the example value is used only in the consumer-side mock. The expression uses a `${}` template syntax referencing a key returned from the state handler's return object, and can be composed with other matchers to enforce type constraints on the injected value. This pattern is the canonical approach for any field whose value is determined by the provider's persistence layer at runtime.

**Tradeoff:** `fromProviderState` requires the state handler to return the injected value as a key-value map, which couples the provider's state handler return contract to the consumer's expression syntax. If multiple consumer interactions reference `${productId}` but the state handler for one consumer returns `productId` as a string and another expects it as a number, the injection silently coerces the value — adding a `regex` or `integer` wrapper around the `fromProviderState` call enforces the type at the pact matcher level and surfaces type mismatches during consumer test execution rather than during provider verification. [official]

```typescript
import {
  PactV4,
  SpecificationVersion,
  fromProviderState,
  uuid,
  string,
  integer,
} from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'OrderDashboard',
  provider: 'OrderService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('OrderService GET /orders/:id — provider-state ID injection', () => {
  it('returns the order detail for an existing order', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      .given('order with ID ord-999 exists', { orderId: 'ord-999' })
      .uponReceiving('GET /orders/:id — fetch existing order detail')
      .withRequest('GET', fromProviderState('/orders/${orderId}', '/orders/ord-999'))
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          // fromProviderState injects the same value into the response body
          id:     fromProviderState('${orderId}', 'ord-999'),
          status: string('PROCESSING'),
          total:  integer(4500),
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/orders/ord-999`);
        const body = await res.json() as { id: string; status: string; total: number };
        expect(res.status).toBe(200);
        // In consumer test the example value is used; provider injects its own ID at verification
        expect(body.id).toBe('ord-999');
        expect(body.status).toBe('PROCESSING');
      });
  });
});

// In the provider state handler (state-handlers.ts):
// 'order with ID ord-999 exists': async (params) => {
//   const order = await db('orders').insert({ status: 'PROCESSING', total: 4500 }).returning('id');
//   return { orderId: order[0].id }; // key matches ${orderId} expression above
// }
```

### Pattern 327 — `pending()` Interaction Flag for Safe Contract Introduction Without Breaking Provider CI [official]

When a consumer team needs to introduce new interactions for functionality that the provider has not yet implemented, publishing those interactions to the Pact Broker with `enablePending: true` on the provider's verifier configuration allows the provider to verify all known pacts without having the pending interactions break the provider's CI build. The pending flag is a dynamic property computed by the Broker at fetch time: a pact is pending for a provider until the provider publishes a successful verification result for it, at which point the Broker automatically clears the pending flag. This approach replaces the older `WIP pacts` feature for individual-interaction-level pending semantics, and is the recommended approach when a consumer wants to communicate upcoming requirements to the provider team without immediately blocking their pipeline.

**Tradeoff:** Pending pacts do not apply to webhook-triggered out-of-band verification builds — the `contract_requiring_verification_published` webhook fires a targeted provider build specifically because a new pact requires verification, and those builds are expected to fail (they are the signal to the provider team that work is required). Teams that rely on webhook-triggered builds as their primary verification pathway will not benefit from the pending flag for those builds; pending only protects the provider's regular scheduled/commit-triggered CI runs. Additionally, once a pact has been verified successfully and the pending flag is cleared, any subsequent regression that re-introduces the failure will cause the build to break — pending only applies to the initial introduction period. [official]

```typescript
// consumer/pact/new-feature.pact.spec.ts
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion, string, integer } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const pact = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'InventoryUI',
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

describe('InventoryService POST /reservations — pending new endpoint', () => {
  it('creates a reservation when sufficient stock exists', async () => {
    await pact
      .addInteraction()
      // Mark as pending: provider has not yet implemented /reservations
      .pending(true)
      .given('SKU sku-abc has 10 units in stock')
      .uponReceiving('POST /reservations — create reservation for in-stock SKU')
      .withRequest('POST', '/reservations', (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({ sku: string('sku-abc'), quantity: integer(2) });
      })
      .willRespondWith(201, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          reservationId: string('res-001'),
          sku:           string('sku-abc'),
          quantity:      integer(2),
          status:        string('RESERVED'),
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const res = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/reservations`, {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify({ sku: 'sku-abc', quantity: 2 }),
        });
        const body = await res.json() as { reservationId: string; status: string };
        expect(res.status).toBe(201);
        expect(body.status).toBe('RESERVED');
      });
  });
});

// Provider verifier (provider/test/verify.ts):
// new VerifierV3({
//   ...
//   enablePending: true,   // <-- allows pending interactions to fail without breaking CI
//   includeWipPactsSince: new Date('2026-01-01'), // also pulls WIP pacts into scope
// }).verifyProvider()
```

---

### Pattern 328 — `contract_requiring_verification_published` Webhook with `providerVersionBranch` Template Parameter for Targeted Branch Verification [official]

The `contract_requiring_verification_published` Pact Broker webhook event (introduced in Broker 2.82.0) replaces the legacy `contract_content_changed` event and provides smarter targeting: it fires once per provider branch/environment combination that is missing a verification result for the newly published pact, rather than firing on every pact publication regardless of verification status. The webhook payload exposes template variables including `${pactbroker.pactUrl}`, `${pactbroker.providerVersionBranch}`, and `${pactbroker.providerVersionNumber}` that can be injected into the CI trigger payload. Configuring a CI pipeline that checks out the provider's `${pactbroker.providerVersionBranch}` branch and runs verification against the single pact URL from `${pactbroker.pactUrl}` ensures that each consumer change immediately triggers the correct provider branch to verify — closing the deployment window gap described in Cycle 43.

**Tradeoff:** The `${pactbroker.providerVersionBranch}` template variable is only populated when the provider has previously published verification results with a `providerVersionBranch` set. Providers that publish results without branch metadata receive a webhook body where `providerVersionBranch` is empty, causing the CI checkout step to fail with a "branch not found" error. Teams migrating from untagged to branch-based workflows must backfill `providerVersionBranch` on at least one successful verification run before the webhook template will resolve correctly — the Pact Broker does not fall back to a default branch when the field is absent. [official]

```typescript
// scripts/trigger-provider-ci.ts — CI API call triggered by the webhook
// This script runs inside a lightweight webhook handler service (e.g., a Lambda)
// that receives the Pact Broker webhook POST and forwards it to the CI system.

interface PactBrokerWebhookPayload {
  consumer:              { name: string; version: string };
  provider:              { name: string; version?: string };
  pactUrl:               string;
  providerVersionBranch: string;
  providerVersionNumber: string;
}

async function triggerProviderCi(payload: PactBrokerWebhookPayload): Promise<void> {
  const ciApiUrl    = process.env.CI_API_URL!;
  const ciApiToken  = process.env.CI_API_TOKEN!;
  const pipelineId  = process.env.PROVIDER_PIPELINE_ID!;

  // Pass pact URL and branch as CI pipeline variables so the provider build
  // only verifies the changed pact, not all pacts (faster, more targeted)
  const triggerBody = {
    ref:       payload.providerVersionBranch || 'main',
    variables: {
      PACT_URL:      payload.pactUrl,
      PACT_CONSUMER: payload.consumer.name,
      // Narrowing: verify only the changed consumer pact, not all registered pacts
      PACT_CONSUMER_VERSION: payload.consumer.version,
    },
  };

  const res = await fetch(`${ciApiUrl}/pipelines/${pipelineId}/trigger`, {
    method:  'POST',
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${ciApiToken}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body:    JSON.stringify(triggerBody),
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error(`CI trigger failed: ${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  }

  console.log(`Triggered provider CI for consumer=${payload.consumer.name} branch=${payload.providerVersionBranch}`);
}
```

---

### Pattern 329 — Multi-Consumer Provider Verification with `{ consumer: 'X', mainBranch: true }` Scoped Selectors to Isolate Per-Consumer Failures [official]

When a single provider has five or more consumers, a verification failure in one consumer's pact should not prevent the provider from deploying if all other consumers' pacts still verify. By constructing the `consumerVersionSelectors` array with one entry per consumer — each scoped with `{ consumer: 'ConsumerName', mainBranch: true }` — the verifier runs a separate verification suite per consumer, and the Pact Broker records per-consumer verification results. The `can-i-deploy` gate then evaluates only the consumers currently deployed to the target environment, so a broken pact for a consumer that is not in that environment does not block deployment. This pattern transforms a monolithic "all consumers pass or nothing deploys" gate into a per-consumer compatibility matrix.

**Tradeoff:** Scoping selectors per consumer increases the number of network round-trips to the Pact Broker during the verification fetch phase, as each selector issues a separate broker query. For providers with more than ten consumers, this can add meaningful latency to the CI startup phase. An alternative is to use a single `{ mainBranch: true }` selector (which fetches all consumers' main-branch pacts in one call) and use `filterConsumerNames` to run separate verification jobs per consumer in parallel CI stages — this parallelizes both the fetch and the verification, avoiding the sequential per-consumer fetch overhead. [official]

```typescript
// provider/test/verify-scoped.ts
import { VerifierV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { startProvider } from '../src/app';

const CONSUMERS = ['CheckoutUI', 'InventoryService', 'ReturnsPortal', 'ReportingService'];

async function runScopedVerification(): Promise<void> {
  const app = await startProvider();

  const verifier = new VerifierV3({
    provider:        'OrderService',
    providerBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:3001',

    // One selector per consumer: each produces an isolated verification result in the Broker
    consumerVersionSelectors: CONSUMERS.map((consumer) => ({
      consumer,
      mainBranch: true,
    })),

    // Also include any version currently deployed to production for each consumer
    // (appended as additional selectors for environment safety)
    // consumerVersionSelectors: [
    //   ...CONSUMERS.map(consumer => ({ consumer, mainBranch: true })),
    //   ...CONSUMERS.map(consumer => ({ consumer, deployedOrReleased: true })),
    // ],

    pactBrokerUrl:         process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL,
    pactBrokerToken:       process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN,
    providerVersion:       process.env.GIT_SHA,
    providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH,
    publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',

    stateHandlers: { /* ... */ },
  });

  await verifier.verifyProvider().finally(() => app.close());
}

runScopedVerification().catch((err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });
```
