**Pattern 682** — `pact-broker create-environment` and Environment Lifecycle Management
```typescript
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

type Environment = 'development' | 'staging' | 'production';

function ensureEnvironmentExists(
  name: Environment,
  displayName: string,
  isProduction: boolean,
  brokerUrl: string,
  token: string,
): void {
  try {
    // create-environment is idempotent — safe to call on every pipeline run
    execSync(
      [
        'pact-broker create-environment',
        `--name "${name}"`,
        `--display-name "${displayName}"`,
        isProduction ? '--production' : '',
        `--broker-base-url "${brokerUrl}"`,
        `--broker-token "${token}"`,
      ].filter(Boolean).join(' '),
      { stdio: 'inherit' },
    );
    console.log(`[pact] Environment '${name}' ensured in broker`);
  } catch (e: unknown) {
    // Broker returns 409 if environment already exists — treat as success
    const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e);
    if (!msg.includes('409')) throw e;
    console.log(`[pact] Environment '${name}' already exists — skipping`);
  }
}

ensureEnvironmentExists('staging', 'Staging', false, process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!, process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!);
ensureEnvironmentExists('production', 'Production', true, process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!, process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!);
```
Tradeoff: Calling `create-environment` idempotently in the pipeline bootstrap step ensures the Pact Broker always has the required environments configured before any `record-deployment` or `can-i-deploy` commands run, preventing those commands from failing with "environment not found" errors when a new environment is added to the CD pipeline — the tradeoff is that marking an environment as `--production` in the broker changes the `can-i-deploy` SLA semantics (production environments require stricter verification coverage), so accidentally flagging a staging environment as production will cause `can-i-deploy` failures for consumers that have not yet been verified against all production-deployed provider versions.

---

**Pattern 683** — `pactfileWriteMode: 'merge'` with Shard-Safe Pact File Accumulation
```typescript
import { PactV4 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

// Each test shard writes to a shard-specific subdirectory, then a post-step merges
const shardId = process.env.TEST_SHARD_INDEX ?? '0';
const shardTotal = process.env.TEST_SHARD_TOTAL ?? '1';

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'CatalogUI',
  provider: 'ProductService',
  dir: `./pacts/shards/shard-${shardId}`,   // isolated per shard
  pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite',             // safe — one shard writes one file
});

// Post-step: merge all shard pact files into a single output (run after all shards complete)
// pact-broker merge-pacts --output ./pacts --dirs ./pacts/shards/*
// The merged file is the one published to the broker

it('fetches product by SKU', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('product SKU-001 exists')
    .uponReceiving('GET /products/SKU-001 — shard safe [CatalogUI]')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/products/SKU-001' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        sku: 'SKU-001',
        name: 'Ergonomic Chair',
        priceCents: 29999,
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const product = await fetchProduct(mockServer.url, 'SKU-001');
      expect(product.sku).toBe('SKU-001');
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: Writing each test shard to an isolated subdirectory with `pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite'` and merging post-shard eliminates the race conditions that occur when multiple shards attempt concurrent writes to the same pact JSON file using `'update'` mode — the tradeoff is that the post-step merge requires the `pact-broker merge-pacts` CLI command to be available and run to completion before the publish step, adding a sequential bottleneck after parallel shard execution; if the merge step is skipped (e.g., due to a CI failure mid-pipeline), an incomplete pact file may be published to the broker, silently dropping interactions from the shards that did not run.

---

**Pattern 684** — `pact-broker generate-uuid` for Stable Interaction IDs Across Re-Runs
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { createHash } from 'crypto';
const { string, integer } = MatchersV3;

// Generate a stable UUID from the interaction description so re-runs produce the same ID
function stableInteractionId(description: string, state: string): string {
  return createHash('sha256')
    .update(`${description}::${state}`)
    .digest('hex')
    .slice(0, 32)
    // format as UUID v4-compatible
    .replace(/^(.{8})(.{4})(.{4})(.{4})(.{12})$/, '$1-$2-$3-$4-$5');
}

const provider = new PactV4({ consumer: 'ShippingUI', provider: 'RateService', dir: './pacts' });

const interactionDescription = 'GET /rates/domestic — standard domestic rate [ShippingUI]';
const interactionState = 'domestic rate table is populated';

it(interactionDescription, async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given(interactionState)
    .uponReceiving(interactionDescription)
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/rates/domestic' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        rateId: string(stableInteractionId(interactionDescription, interactionState)),
        baseRateCents: integer(599),
        currency: string('USD'),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const rate = await fetchDomesticRate(mockServer.url);
      expect(rate.baseRateCents).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: Deriving response IDs from a deterministic hash of the interaction description and state ensures that repeated pact generation runs produce the same pact JSON output (byte-for-byte stable), preventing unnecessary pact republications to the broker when no consumer code has changed — the tradeoff is that using a hash of the description as the example `rateId` means the consumer's `executeTest` block receives a hash string rather than a realistic rate ID, so consumer code that validates the format of the returned ID (e.g., `expect(rate.rateId).toMatch(/^[0-9]+$/)`) will fail, requiring the example value to be a realistic-looking ID rather than a hash.

---

**Pattern 685** — `pact-broker webhooks test` for Webhook Configuration Verification in CI
```typescript
import axios from 'axios';

interface WebhookTestResult {
  webhookId: string;
  success: boolean;
  statusCode: number;
  responseBody: string;
}

async function testWebhook(
  brokerUrl: string,
  token: string,
  webhookId: string,
): Promise<WebhookTestResult> {
  const response = await axios.post(
    `${brokerUrl}/webhooks/${webhookId}/execute`,
    {},
    {
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
      validateStatus: () => true,  // don't throw on non-2xx so we can inspect result
    },
  );

  const success = response.status >= 200 && response.status < 300;
  console.log(
    `[pact-webhook-test] Webhook ${webhookId}: ${success ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL'} (HTTP ${response.status})`,
  );

  return {
    webhookId,
    success,
    statusCode: response.status,
    responseBody: JSON.stringify(response.data).slice(0, 200),
  };
}

// Run in pipeline to verify all registered webhooks are reachable
const WEBHOOK_IDS = (process.env.PACT_WEBHOOK_IDS ?? '').split(',').filter(Boolean);

Promise.all(
  WEBHOOK_IDS.map((id) =>
    testWebhook(process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!, process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!, id.trim()),
  ),
).then((results) => {
  const failures = results.filter((r) => !r.success);
  if (failures.length > 0) {
    console.error('[pact-webhook-test] Failed webhooks:', failures);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  console.log(`[pact-webhook-test] All ${results.length} webhooks reachable`);
});
```
Tradeoff: Executing registered webhooks via the Pact Broker's `/webhooks/{id}/execute` endpoint in a scheduled CI job provides early warning when CI provider endpoints rotate (new URLs, expired tokens, IP allowlist changes) before a real `contract_content_changed` event fires — the tradeoff is that the broker's webhook test endpoint fires the webhook with a synthetic test payload that does not represent a real contract change, so CI systems that trigger a full provider verification on webhook receipt will run a potentially unnecessary verification suite, increasing CI minutes consumed by the health-check job.

---

### Community Gotchas

**GCL-351** — `withRequest` `query` Object Values Must Be Strings, Not Numbers
Why this matters: The Pact V4 `withRequest` API accepts a `query` object where all values must be strings (since HTTP query strings are inherently string-typed). When developers pass numeric values — e.g., `query: { page: 1, limit: 20 }` — TypeScript's structural typing may not raise an error because some Pact type definitions accept `Record<string, string | number>`. At runtime, Pact serialises the numeric values correctly, but the mock server's request matching uses strict string comparison. A consumer request of `?page=1&limit=20` is matched against the string representation, which succeeds. However, when the provider verifier receives the pact file and replays the request, the query parameter type annotation in the pact JSON may cause some verifier implementations to reject the interaction as malformed, producing an opaque "interaction could not be parsed" error that does not indicate the cause.
Fix: Always declare all query parameter values as strings in `withRequest`: `query: { page: '1', limit: '20' }`. Add an ESLint rule (`pact/query-string-values`) or a type-safe wrapper function `queryParams(params: Record<string, string>)` that enforces string values at compile time. Include a comment in the codebase's pact test template noting that query parameter values are always strings regardless of their semantic numeric meaning.

---

**GCL-352** — Provider Verification Producing Empty `_links` in Broker Results When `provider` Name Has Spaces
Why this matters: Some teams name their services with human-readable display names that include spaces (e.g., `provider: 'Order Service'` instead of `'OrderService'`). When the Pact Broker stores the verification result for a provider name containing spaces, the broker generates a HAL link URL by URL-encoding the spaces as `%20`. The Pact Broker UI renders the name correctly, but downstream tools that consume the broker's API (e.g., Slack webhook formatters, internal dashboards) that construct URLs by simple string concatenation (without URL-encoding) produce broken links. More critically, `can-i-deploy --pacticipant "Order Service"` may fail on some CLI versions because the pacticipant name resolver does not consistently URL-encode the name before querying the broker API.
Fix: Standardise all provider and consumer names in the Pact configuration as PascalCase identifiers without spaces (e.g., `OrderService`, `CheckoutUI`). Add a validation step in `bin/hooks/pact-pre-publish.sh` that checks the `provider` and `consumer` fields in all pact JSON files match a regex of `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*$` before publishing. Update internal service catalogues to use the PascalCase pact name as the canonical identifier.

---

**GCL-353** — `stateHandlers` Using `async/await` Without Returning the Promise Causes Unhandled Rejections
Why this matters: Provider state handlers declared as `async` functions must be awaited by the Pact verifier for setup and teardown to complete before the interaction fires. When a developer writes a state handler as an arrow function that calls an `async` helper but forgets to `return` or `await` it — e.g., `'user exists': () => { setupUser(); }` where `setupUser` is `async` — the state handler returns a resolved `Promise<void>` immediately without waiting for the database write to complete. The interaction fires against an empty database, and the provider returns a 404 or 500. The test failure message reports a response body mismatch rather than indicating the root cause, and the unhandled rejection from `setupUser` may surface in the Jest output after all pact interactions have already been reported as failed.
Fix: Always write state handlers as `async` functions that `return` or `await` all async operations: `'user exists': async () => { await setupUser('usr-1'); }`. Enable Jest's `--detectOpenHandles` flag on provider verification runs to surface dangling promises that indicate a missing `await`. Add a TypeScript type annotation on the `stateHandlers` map: `stateHandlers: Record<string, () => Promise<void>>` to cause a compile-time error when a handler returns `void` instead of `Promise<void>`.

---

**GCL-354** — `enablePending: true` Without `includeWipPactsSince` Results in No WIP Pacts Being Verified
Why this matters: Teams that set `enablePending: true` in the Verifier configuration without also setting `includeWipPactsSince` will find that pending pacts from new consumers are never added to the verification run. In the Pact Broker, a "pending" pact and a "WIP" pact are distinct concepts: pending pacts are ones that have been previously published but never successfully verified; WIP pacts are pacts from consumer branches that have never been part of a formal verification at all. The `enablePending` flag unlocks pending pacts; the `includeWipPactsSince` flag unlocks WIP pacts. Without `includeWipPactsSince`, brand-new consumer branches publishing their first pact will never appear in the provider's verification run, leaving the consumer team unable to get early feedback on whether their new contract is compatible with the provider.
Fix: Always pair `enablePending: true` with `includeWipPactsSince: rollingDate(30)` (a date 30 days in the past) to ensure both pending and WIP pacts are included in provider verification. Document in the team's pact onboarding guide that a new consumer's pact will only appear in provider CI after both flags are set and the consumer has published at least one pact version. Use the Pact Broker's "matrix" UI to confirm a new consumer appears in the verification matrix within one provider CI run of publishing their first pact.

---

**GCL-355** — Consumer Pact Test Passing Because Mock Server Ignores Extra Request Headers
Why this matters: The Pact mock server, by default, does not perform strict matching on request headers — it only checks that the headers declared in `withRequest.headers` are present with the correct values. Headers present in the actual consumer request but not declared in the pact are silently ignored. This means a consumer that sends a required header (e.g., `X-Tenant-Id: tenant-abc`) will have the pact test pass even if the `withRequest.headers` declaration omits `X-Tenant-Id`. At provider verification time, the pact does not assert that `X-Tenant-Id` must be sent, so the provider is never tested against tenant-scoped routing logic. When the provider is deployed to production, requests from the consumer that include `X-Tenant-Id` route correctly, but the contract test provides no protection against a future provider change that breaks tenant-header routing.
Fix: Explicitly declare all headers that are functionally required by the provider in `withRequest.headers`, not just `Content-Type` and `Authorization`. For tenant-scoped APIs, add `'X-Tenant-Id': string('tenant-abc')` (using a `string()` matcher so any valid tenant ID passes) to every interaction that exercises tenant-aware endpoints. Enable Pact's strict header matching mode where available, or add a consumer-side assertion inside `executeTest` that the request function correctly includes the header before the mock server receives it.

**Pattern 686** — `fromProviderState()` for Injecting Auto-Assigned Database IDs into Response Contracts
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { fromProviderState, like, string } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'ShipmentService',
  provider: 'WarehouseService',
  dir: path.resolve(__dirname, '../../pacts'),
});

it('should return the auto-assigned pallet slot ID for zone A', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('a pallet slot will be auto-assigned in zone A', { zone: 'A' })
    .uponReceiving('a POST request to assign a pallet slot in zone A')
    .withRequest({
      method: 'POST',
      path: '/pallets',
      body: { zone: 'A', weightKg: like(250) },
    })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 201,
      body: {
        slotId:     fromProviderState('${slotId}', 'SLOT-TEST-001'),
        zone:       string('A'),
        assignedAt: like(1714800000),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new WarehouseClient(mockServer.url);
      const result = await client.assignSlot({ zone: 'A', weightKg: 250 });
      expect(result.slotId).toMatch(/^SLOT-/);
    });
});
// Consumer mock uses 'SLOT-TEST-001'; provider stateHandlers return the real DB-generated slotId.
```
Tradeoff: `fromProviderState()` allows the consumer contract to reference provider-generated IDs without hardcoding them, making the contract resilient to provider-side UUID generation strategies — the tradeoff is that the interpolation key (`${slotId}`) must match the return-map key in the provider's `stateHandlers` exactly (case-sensitive), and a mismatch causes the Rust core to substitute an empty string during provider verification rather than raising a missing-key error, producing a false-green consumer suite alongside a cryptic content-mismatch failure in the provider run.

**Pattern 687** — `arrayContaining()` for Mandatory Feature-Subset Assertions on Subscription Plans
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { arrayContaining, string } = MatchersV3;

it('should confirm the Enterprise plan includes mandatory compliance features', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('the Enterprise subscription plan is active')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for Enterprise plan feature list')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/plans/enterprise/features' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        planId:   string('enterprise'),
        features: arrayContaining([
          string('sso'),
          string('audit-log'),
          string('custom-roles'),
          string('data-residency'),
        ]),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new BillingClient(mockServer.url);
      const plan = await client.getPlanFeatures('enterprise');
      expect(plan.features).toContain('sso');
      expect(plan.features).toContain('audit-log');
    });
});
// arrayContaining passes when all listed elements are present regardless of ordering
// or the presence of additional provider-defined features.
```
Tradeoff: `arrayContaining()` allows the provider to add new features to the Enterprise plan without breaking the consumer contract — the tradeoff is that it imposes no upper bound on the feature count, so a provider that accidentally includes features from a higher-tier plan passes verification; for licensing accuracy, supplement the contract test with an integration test asserting exact set equality between the plan's feature list and the authoritative entitlement registry.

**Pattern 688** — `eachKeyMatches()` + `eachValueMatches()` for Validated Currency Exchange-Rate Maps
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { eachKeyMatches, eachValueMatches, regex, decimal } = MatchersV3;

it('should return a USD exchange-rate map with ISO 4217 keys and decimal values', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('live FX rates are available for USD base')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for USD-based exchange rates')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/fx-rates', query: { base: 'USD' } })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        base: 'USD',
        rates: eachKeyMatches(
          eachValueMatches(
            { EUR: 0.92, GBP: 0.79, JPY: 154.3 },
            decimal(0.92)
          ),
          regex('[A-Z]{3}', 'EUR')
        ),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new FxClient(mockServer.url);
      const rates = await client.getRates('USD');
      expect(Object.keys(rates.rates).every((k) => /^[A-Z]{3}$/.test(k))).toBe(true);
    });
});
// Validates: every key is a 3-letter uppercase ISO currency code AND
// every value is a decimal — irrespective of how many currencies the provider returns.
```
Tradeoff: Composing `eachKeyMatches()` and `eachValueMatches()` creates a fully structural contract for the exchange-rate map that allows the provider to add or remove currencies freely — the tradeoff is that both matchers require Pact Specification V3 or higher, and when applied against a V2 provider verifier they silently degrade to exact equality on the generate-value object, rendering the contract test useless for any dynamically keyed provider response.

**Pattern 689** — `constrainedArrayLike()` to Enforce Minimum and Maximum Dashboard Widget Counts
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { constrainedArrayLike, like, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

it('should return between 1 and 20 dashboard widgets for user u-42', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('user u-42 has 8 configured dashboard widgets')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for user u-42 dashboard widgets')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/dashboard/widgets', query: { userId: 'u-42' } })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        widgets: constrainedArrayLike(
          {
            widgetId: like('wgt-001'),
            type:     string('chart'),
            title:    like('Revenue Overview'),
            position: integer(0),
          },
          1,   // min
          20   // max
        ),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new DashboardClient(mockServer.url);
      const result = await client.getWidgets('u-42');
      expect(result.widgets.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
      expect(result.widgets.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(20);
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: `constrainedArrayLike()` bakes the consumer's pagination expectation directly into the pact so that a provider returning more than 20 widgets fails verification immediately — the tradeoff is that the Pact mock server generates exactly `min` (1) widget during consumer testing, leaving the consumer's rendering logic for 10 or 20 widgets unexercised by the contract test; those branches require explicit unit tests.

**Pattern 690** — `messageProviders` Map with Real Production Event Producers for Kafka Contracts
```typescript
import { MessageProviderPact } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { buildOrderConfirmedEvent } from '../src/events/orderConfirmed';

const messagePact = new MessageProviderPact({
  messageProviders: {
    'an OrderConfirmed event for a standard order': async () =>
      buildOrderConfirmedEvent({
        orderId:    'ORD-500',
        customerId: 'CUST-99',
        totalCents: 5999,
        currency:   'USD',
        items:      [{ sku: 'SKU-1', qty: 2, priceCents: 2999 }],
      }),
    'an OrderConfirmed event for a VIP high-value order': async () =>
      buildOrderConfirmedEvent({
        orderId:    'ORD-9999',
        customerId: 'CUST-VIP',
        totalCents: 250000,
        currency:   'USD',
        items:      [{ sku: 'SKU-GOLD', qty: 1, priceCents: 250000 }],
      }),
  },
  provider:               'OrderService',
  pactBrokerUrl:          process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
  pactBrokerToken:        process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
  publishVerificationResults: process.env.CI === 'true',
  providerVersion:        process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
  providerVersionBranch:  process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
  consumerVersionSelectors: [
    { mainBranch: true },
    { deployedOrReleased: true },
  ],
});

describe('OrderConfirmed message provider verification', () => {
  it('verifies all consumer message interactions', () => messagePact.verify());
});
```
Tradeoff: Wiring `messageProviders` to the real `buildOrderConfirmedEvent` function ensures the verified payload structure exactly matches what the production Kafka producer emits — the tradeoff is that the `messageProviders` key must match the consumer test's interaction `description` field character-for-character (including punctuation); any mismatch causes the provider to skip the interaction silently rather than reporting a missing handler, leaving an unverified interaction in the matrix with no error surfaced during the provider run.

**Pattern 691** — Transaction-Rollback `beforeEach`/`afterEach` for Fully Isolated Provider State
```typescript
import { Verifier } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { db } from '../src/db';
import { seedUser, clearUsers } from '../test/fixtures/users';

const verifier = new Verifier({
  providerBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:4000',
  provider: 'UserService',
  providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
  providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH ?? 'main',
  stateHandlers: {
    'user alice exists with admin role': {
      setup: async () => {
        await clearUsers();
        await seedUser({ id: 'alice', role: 'admin', active: true });
      },
      teardown: async () => { await clearUsers(); },
    },
    'no users exist': {
      setup:    async () => { await clearUsers(); },
      teardown: async () => { await clearUsers(); },
    },
  },
  beforeEach: async () => { await db.beginTransaction(); },
  afterEach:  async () => { await db.rollbackTransaction(); },
  publishVerificationResults: process.env.CI === 'true',
});

await verifier.verifyProvider();
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping each pact interaction in a transaction rollback ensures no database state leaks between interactions, eliminating order-dependent failures when the broker replays interactions in non-deterministic sequence — the tradeoff is that this pattern requires the database driver to support nested transactions or savepoints; if the driver auto-commits on DDL statements (as PostgreSQL does with `CREATE TABLE`), the rollback silently no-ops and the isolation guarantee is lost without any error, causing intermittent test failures that are extremely difficult to diagnose.

**Pattern 692** — `pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite'` Combined with Pre-Run `pacts/` Directory Cleanup
```typescript
import { PactV4 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

const PACTS_DIR = path.resolve(__dirname, '../../pacts');

// Clean the output directory before the test suite runs to eliminate stale interactions
beforeAll(() => {
  if (fs.existsSync(PACTS_DIR)) {
    fs.rmSync(PACTS_DIR, { recursive: true, force: true });
  }
  fs.mkdirSync(PACTS_DIR, { recursive: true });
});

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'NotificationService',
  provider: 'UserPreferencesAPI',
  dir: PACTS_DIR,
  pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite',  // regenerate from scratch — no stale interaction merging
  logLevel: 'error',
});

it('should retrieve email preference for user maria', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('user maria has email notifications enabled')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for maria email preference')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/users/maria/preferences/email' })
    .willRespondWith({ status: 200, body: { userId: 'maria', emailEnabled: true } })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new PrefsClient(mockServer.url);
      const pref = await client.getEmailPref('maria');
      expect(pref.emailEnabled).toBe(true);
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: `'overwrite'` + pre-run directory cleanup guarantees the published pact contains exactly the interactions in the current test suite, with no residue from deleted tests — the tradeoff is that it cannot coexist safely with interactions for the same provider-consumer pair split across multiple Jest test files, because each file's `beforeAll` cleanup would erase the previous file's interactions; consolidate all interactions for a single provider-consumer pair into one test file when using `'overwrite'` mode.

**Pattern 693** — `create-environment` + `can-i-deploy` + `record-deployment` as a Three-Step CD Gate
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Complete deployment gate pipeline using Pact Broker CLI
set -euo pipefail

BROKER_URL="${PACT_BROKER_URL}"
BROKER_TOKEN="${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}"
ENVIRONMENT="${DEPLOY_ENVIRONMENT}"
PACTICIPANT="${SERVICE_NAME}"
VERSION="${GIT_COMMIT}"

# Step 1: Ensure the environment is registered (idempotent)
pact-broker create-environment \
  --name "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --display-name "${ENVIRONMENT^}" \
  --broker-base-url "${BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token "${BROKER_TOKEN}" \
  --no-production 2>/dev/null || true

# Step 2: Gate deployment on contract compatibility
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant "${PACTICIPANT}" \
  --version "${VERSION}" \
  --to-environment "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --broker-base-url "${BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token "${BROKER_TOKEN}"

# Step 3: Run the actual deployment (insert real deploy command here)
echo "Deploying ${PACTICIPANT}@${VERSION} to ${ENVIRONMENT}..."

# Step 4: Record deployment only after deploy + health check succeed
pact-broker record-deployment \
  --pacticipant "${PACTICIPANT}" \
  --version "${VERSION}" \
  --environment "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --broker-base-url "${BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token "${BROKER_TOKEN}"
```
Tradeoff: The three-step sequence ensures `record-deployment` is always a trailing confirmation of a successful deploy rather than a leading assumption, keeping the Pact matrix accurate — the tradeoff is that `create-environment` requires Pact Broker CLI 1.64.0+ and is absent from older CLI versions, so teams on legacy tooling must pre-register environments via the broker web UI or API before this script can succeed.

**Pattern 694** — `requestFilter` Middleware for Injecting Tenant-ID and Auth Headers in Multi-Tenant Providers
```typescript
import { Verifier } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import type { IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from 'http';

const verifier = new Verifier({
  providerBaseUrl: process.env.PROVIDER_BASE_URL!,
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
  providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
  pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
  requestFilter: (
    req: IncomingMessage,
    _res: ServerResponse,
    next: () => void
  ): void => {
    // Auth header required by all routes
    req.headers['authorization']     = `Bearer ${process.env.VERIFIER_SERVICE_TOKEN}`;
    // Multi-tenancy header required by every API endpoint
    req.headers['x-tenant-id']       = process.env.PACT_TENANT_ID ?? 'test-tenant-001';
    // Disable rate limiting for the CI verifier service account
    req.headers['x-bypass-ratelimit'] = 'pact-verifier';
    next();
  },
  publishVerificationResults: process.env.CI === 'true',
});

await verifier.verifyProvider();
```
Tradeoff: Centralizing multi-header injection in a single `requestFilter` keeps all cross-cutting auth concerns DRY and eliminates repetition across every `stateHandlers` function — the tradeoff is that `requestFilter` applies identical headers to every interaction uniformly, so interactions designed to test unauthenticated, wrong-tenant, or rate-limited error paths will always receive valid headers and can never verify the provider's rejection logic through this mechanism; those paths need separate out-of-band provider tests.

**Pattern 695** — `{ branch: 'feat/...', consumer: '...' }` Selector for Cross-Team Feature Coordination
```typescript
import { Verifier } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

// During a cross-team sprint, WebApp publishes pacts on 'feat/checkout-v2'.
// CheckoutService must verify them before merging its own feature branch.
const verifier = new Verifier({
  providerBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:5000',
  provider: 'CheckoutService',
  providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
  providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
  pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
  pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
  consumerVersionSelectors: [
    { matchingBranch: true },
    { branch: 'feat/checkout-v2', consumer: 'WebApp' },
    { deployedOrReleased: true },
    { mainBranch: true },
  ],
  enablePending: true,
  includeWipPactsSince: new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
    .toISOString().slice(0, 10),
  publishVerificationResults: process.env.CI === 'true',
});

await verifier.verifyProvider();
```
Tradeoff: An explicit branch+consumer selector ensures the cross-team feature pact is verified on every provider CI run regardless of branch-name similarity — the tradeoff is that the hard-coded branch name must be removed from the provider configuration once the feature branch is merged; if left in place after branch deletion, the selector silently finds no pact on every run and the verifier log shows a benign "no pact found" warning that teams tend to ignore, masking legitimate future pact resolution failures.

**Pattern 696** — `nullValue()` Matcher for Explicit Null Contracts on Conditional Optional Fields
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { like, string, nullValue } = MatchersV3;

it('should return null shippingAddress for digital-only orders', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('order ORD-DIG-001 contains only digital items')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for order ORD-DIG-001')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/orders/ORD-DIG-001' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        orderId:         string('ORD-DIG-001'),
        totalCents:      like(1999),
        itemType:        string('digital'),
        shippingAddress: nullValue(),   // explicitly null — not absent, not empty object
        downloadUrl:     like('https://cdn.example.com/dl/token-abc'),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new OrderClient(mockServer.url);
      const order = await client.getOrder('ORD-DIG-001');
      expect(order.shippingAddress).toBeNull();
      expect(order.downloadUrl).toBeDefined();
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: `nullValue()` precisely contracts that `shippingAddress` must be `null` (not absent, not `{}`, not `undefined`) for digital orders, preventing the provider from silently changing the null-field representation — the tradeoff is that if the API evolves to omit the field entirely (field removal instead of null-coalescing), the contract test fails even though most consumer code treats `null` and `undefined` identically via optional chaining, requiring a pact update to switch from `nullValue()` to an optional field matcher.

**Pattern 697** — `includes()` Substring Matcher for Semantic Keyword Assertions in Error Messages
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { includes, like, integer } = MatchersV3;

it('should return 422 with an error message mentioning "quantity" for out-of-stock items', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('catalog item SKU-SOLD is out of stock')
    .uponReceiving('a POST request to add an out-of-stock item to cart')
    .withRequest({
      method: 'POST',
      path: '/cart/items',
      body: { sku: 'SKU-SOLD', quantity: 2 },
    })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 422,
      body: {
        errorCode: like('OUT_OF_STOCK'),
        message:   includes('quantity'),   // must mention the offending field
        available: integer(0),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new CartClient(mockServer.url);
      await expect(client.addItem('SKU-SOLD', 2))
        .rejects.toThrow(expect.objectContaining({ statusCode: 422 }));
    });
});
```
Tradeoff: `includes()` prevents the provider from stripping key semantic context (the field name) from validation error messages without triggering a contract failure — the tradeoff is that it is permissive about surrounding wording, so a provider changing `"Requested quantity exceeds available stock"` to `"The quantity field is required"` passes verification even though the semantic meaning shifted from stock-level to required-field, meaning `includes()` is appropriate only when presence of the keyword is the consumer's sole concern rather than the full error meaning.

**Pattern 698** — `equal()` Exact Matcher for Enum Discriminator Fields the Consumer Switches On
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { equal, like } = MatchersV3;

it('should return exact status "PENDING_FULFILLMENT" for a newly placed order', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('order ORD-888 was just placed and awaits fulfillment')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for order ORD-888 status')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/orders/ORD-888/status' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        orderId:     like('ORD-888'),
        orderStatus: equal('PENDING_FULFILLMENT'),   // consumer branches on this exact string
        updatedAt:   like(1714800000),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new OrderClient(mockServer.url);
      const result = await client.getOrderStatus('ORD-888');
      expect(result.orderStatus).toBe('PENDING_FULFILLMENT');
    });
});
// Use equal() — not like() — for discriminators where the consumer renders
// a different UI component or takes a different code path per exact value.
```
Tradeoff: `equal()` ensures that a provider rename of `PENDING_FULFILLMENT` to `AWAITING_FULFILLMENT` fails verification immediately rather than silently passing — the tradeoff is that each permitted enum value requires its own consumer test interaction, and every new status value the consumer must handle requires a pact update before the provider can ship it, creating a tight cross-team coordination dependency for every enum extension.

---

**Pattern 699** — `date()`, `time()`, and `timestamp()` V3 Matchers for ISO 8601 Temporal Field Contracts
```typescript
import { PactV4, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
const { date, time, timestamp, like } = MatchersV3;

it('should return maintenance window with validly formatted ISO 8601 temporal fields', async () => {
  await provider
    .addInteraction()
    .given('a maintenance window is scheduled for 2026-06-01 02:00 UTC')
    .uponReceiving('a GET request for the next scheduled maintenance window')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/maintenance/upcoming' })
    .willRespondWith({
      status: 200,
      body: {
        windowId:    like('MW-042'),
        startDate:   date("yyyy-MM-dd",           '2026-06-01'),
        startTime:   time("HH:mm:ssXXX",          '02:00:00+00:00'),
        scheduledAt: timestamp("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX", '2026-05-15T09:00:00+00:00'),
        durationMin: like(120),
      },
    })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new MaintenanceClient(mockServer.url);
      const win = await client.getUpcoming();
      expect(new Date(win.scheduledAt).getFullYear()).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2026);
    });
});
// Format patterns follow Java DateTimeFormatter syntax (used by Pact Rust core),
// not JavaScript Intl.DateTimeFormat — document this distinction for the team.
```
Tradeoff: Using `date()`, `time()`, and `timestamp()` with explicit format strings enforces that the provider returns parseable temporal strings the consumer can reliably handle — the tradeoff is that the format pattern language is Java's `DateTimeFormatter` (e.g., `yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX`), not JavaScript's; an incorrect pattern fails provider verification with a generic "unable to match date" error that does not identify the offending field, requiring manual inspection of every temporal field in the pact to locate the mismatch.

---

**Pattern 700** — `can-i-deploy --retry-while-unknown` for Webhook-Triggered Asynchronous Verification Polling
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Consumer CI: poll can-i-deploy until the provider verification result arrives
# (triggered by broker webhook → provider CI pipeline → verification publish)
set -euo pipefail

CONSUMER="${SERVICE_NAME}"
VERSION="${GIT_COMMIT}"
ENVIRONMENT="${DEPLOY_ENVIRONMENT:-staging}"

# Poll every 10 seconds for up to 10 minutes (60 retries)
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant      "${CONSUMER}" \
  --version          "${VERSION}" \
  --to-environment   "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --retry-while-unknown 60 \
  --retry-interval   10 \
  --broker-base-url  "${PACT_BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token     "${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}" \
  --output json \
| tee /tmp/cid-result.json

DEPLOYABLE=$(jq -r '.summary.deployable' /tmp/cid-result.json)
if [[ "${DEPLOYABLE}" != "true" ]]; then
  echo "can-i-deploy BLOCKED or timed out:" >&2
  jq '.matrix' /tmp/cid-result.json >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "can-i-deploy PASSED: ${CONSUMER}@${VERSION} can deploy to ${ENVIRONMENT}"
```
Tradeoff: `--retry-while-unknown` converts `can-i-deploy` into a synchronous deployment gate that waits for webhook-triggered provider verification to complete before the consumer pipeline proceeds — the tradeoff is that if the broker webhook fails to deliver (misconfigured URL, network partition, provider CI outage) or the provider takes longer than the total retry budget, `can-i-deploy` times out and exits 1 unconditionally, blocking the consumer merge even when verification would have passed; add broker webhook delivery monitoring so delivery failures are caught before they block consumer pipelines.

### Community Gotchas

**GCL-356** — `fromProviderState()` Template Key Mismatch Causes Empty-String Injection at Provider Verification
Why this matters: The `fromProviderState('${paramKey}', 'fallback')` expression requires `paramKey` to exactly match the key in the object returned by the provider's `stateHandlers` function. A one-character difference — such as `slotId` vs `slot_id`, or `orderId` vs `orderID` — causes the Pact Rust core to resolve the template variable to an empty string at provider verification time instead of raising a "parameter not found" error. The consumer test passes because the mock server uses `'fallback'`; the provider verification sends an empty string to the real endpoint, which typically causes a 400 or a database lookup miss rather than an explicit pact mismatch error. Teams diagnose this as a provider regression and waste hours before finding the key-naming inconsistency.
Fix: Establish a team-wide naming convention for state-handler parameter keys (e.g., always camelCase) and enforce it in code review. Write a provider-side unit test that calls each `stateHandlers` function, captures the return object, and asserts it contains every key referenced by `fromProviderState()` expressions in the published pact JSON. Add a post-verification check that scans the verifier output for interactions where the response body contains empty strings in ID fields, failing the CI step with a targeted "possible fromProviderState key mismatch" message.

---

**GCL-357** — `pactfileWriteMode: 'update'` Accumulates Deleted Interactions Across Test Runs
Why this matters: The default `pactfileWriteMode: 'update'` in pact-js merges each test run's interactions into the existing on-disk pact file rather than regenerating it. When a developer deletes a consumer test covering an endpoint the provider has since removed, the corresponding interaction persists in the pact file from the last time it was written. That ghost interaction is published to the broker, and the provider must verify it. If the endpoint no longer exists, provider verification fails on an interaction that no consumer code uses — blocking the provider's deployment with no actionable fix short of manually deleting the interaction from the broker. The deleted test leaves no trace in the consumer codebase, so the mismatch between the published pact and the consumer's actual behaviour is invisible during code review.
Fix: Set `pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite'` and add `rm -rf pacts/` as a CI pre-step before running consumer tests. This ensures each CI run produces a pact file reflecting only the currently active test interactions. For consumer suites split across multiple test files for the same provider, use a Jest `globalSetup` script to clear the pacts directory once before any worker starts, preventing per-file overwrites from competing with each other.

---

**GCL-358** — `stateHandlers` Defined as Synchronous Functions Without Return Values Cause Silent Race Conditions
Why this matters: pact-js invokes each `stateHandlers` function and waits for the returned `Promise` to resolve before forwarding the verification request to the provider. If a handler is defined as a plain synchronous function that calls an async `seedDb()` without `await` and without returning the resulting promise — e.g., `'user exists': () => { seedDb(); }` — pact-js receives `undefined` from the handler, treats the state setup as complete, and immediately forwards the request. The provider processes the request against an empty or partially initialized database. The verification fails with a body content mismatch, but the error message shows a data difference rather than a timing issue, causing teams to investigate the provider logic instead of the test setup.
Fix: Declare all `stateHandlers` as `async` functions, use `await` on every async operation, and explicitly return the state descriptor object: `'user exists': async () => { await seedDb({ userId: 'u-1' }); return { userId: 'u-1' }; }`. Add TypeScript's `StateHandlers` type annotation from `@pact-foundation/pact` to the handlers map so the compiler catches functions that do not return `Promise<void | unknown>`. Add a CI lint rule that rejects any state handler function body containing an async call without a preceding `await`.

---

**GCL-359** — `providerVersionBranch` Omitted from Verifier Causes All Pacts to Remain Pending Indefinitely
Why this matters: The Pact Broker's pending-pact graduation mechanism requires the provider to publish verification results tagged with a `providerVersionBranch`. When `providerVersionBranch` is omitted from the Verifier configuration, the broker receives verification results with no branch association and cannot graduate any pact from "pending" to "verified." Every pact remains in pending status forever, which means `enablePending: true` silently neutralizes all verification failures — the provider build never fails on any broken interaction, including ones that represent real breaking changes to deployed consumer integrations. The provider team gains false confidence that everything is green while the broker matrix accumulates permanently unverified interactions.
Fix: Always set `providerVersionBranch` explicitly and add a startup guard: `const branch = process.env.GIT_BRANCH?.replace('refs/heads/', ''); if (!branch) throw new Error('GIT_BRANCH is required for broker branch tracking');`. Export the branch name reliably in CI (GitHub Actions: `env: GIT_BRANCH: ${{ github.ref_name }}`). After enabling the fix, manually inspect the broker matrix for pacts still in permanent pending status and trigger a fresh provider verification run to establish the first branch-associated successful result for each.

---

**GCL-360** — Hardcoded Feature-Branch Selectors Left in Provider Config After Merge Block Future Verification
Why this matters: Adding a `{ branch: 'feat/checkout-v2', consumer: 'WebApp' }` selector to the provider's `consumerVersionSelectors` array for a cross-team sprint is correct during development but must be removed once the feature branch is merged. If the selector is left in place after the branch is deleted from the broker (either by retention policy or by a manual delete), every provider CI run logs a benign "no pact found for branch feat/checkout-v2" warning. Teams habituate to ignoring this warning. When a future legitimate pact-resolution failure occurs for an unrelated consumer, its error is buried in the same "no pact found" warning category and goes unnoticed until a consumer is blocked from deploying.
Fix: Treat feature-branch selectors as temporary and track their removal as a follow-up ticket created at the time the feature branch PR is merged. Store all provider `consumerVersionSelectors` in a version-controlled configuration file with inline comments indicating the owning JIRA ticket and planned removal date. Add a CI step that reads the selectors file and fails if any selector contains a `branch` key whose value does not correspond to an active Git branch in the remote repository, automating detection of stale branch selectors before they become invisible noise.

## Provider State Discovery Endpoint

The Pact Broker exposes a provider state discovery endpoint that returns all provider states referenced across active consumer pacts for a given provider. Validating your `stateHandlers` map against this list at CI startup prevents silent gaps where a consumer references a state the provider never implemented.

```typescript
// validate-state-handlers.ts — run in beforeAll or as a CI pre-flight check
interface BrokerProviderStates {
  providerStates: string[];
}

export async function validateStateHandlers(
  stateHandlers: Record<string, StateHandler>,
  providerName: string,
  brokerUrl: string,
  brokerToken: string
): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(
    `${brokerUrl}/providers/${encodeURIComponent(providerName)}/provider-states`,
    { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${brokerToken}` } }
  );
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Broker returned ${response.status} — check PACT_BROKER_TOKEN`);
  }
  const data = (await response.json()) as BrokerProviderStates;

  const requiredStates = new Set(data.providerStates);
  const implementedStates = new Set(Object.keys(stateHandlers));
  const missing = [...requiredStates].filter((s) => !implementedStates.has(s));

  if (missing.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(
      `${missing.length} provider state(s) referenced by consumers have no handler:\n` +
        missing.map((s) => `  • "${s}"`).join('\n')
    );
  }
}

// Usage in Jest/Vitest provider test
beforeAll(async () => {
  await validateStateHandlers(stateHandlers, 'OrderService', brokerUrl, brokerToken);
});
```

**Why this matters:** Consumer pacts reference provider states by string. When a consumer adds a new state and the provider team is unaware, verification silently passes at the consumer side (the consumer test has no handler requirement) but fails at the provider side — often discovered only in production when the provider state setup is skipped. The discovery endpoint surfaces this mismatch early.

> [community] The endpoint reflects the state of currently-published pacts only. If `record-deployment` is not called after each deploy, the endpoint may return stale states from retracted pact versions. Always pair discovery validation with a `can-i-deploy` gate. — GCL-361

## Extended Verification Results  [community]

Pact Broker 2.100+ (PactFlow) captures client language and framework metadata from verification results. The `@pact-foundation/pact` verifier automatically emits this metadata when `publishVerificationResult: true` is set. This enables PactFlow dashboards to display which runtime produced each verification.

```typescript
// provider.pact.spec.ts — metadata is emitted automatically with these options
const verifier = new Verifier({
  provider: 'OrderService',
  providerBaseUrl: `http://localhost:${port}`,
  pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL!,
  pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!,
  publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
  providerVersion: process.env.GIT_COMMIT!,
  providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH!,
  // Extended results: pact-js emits { clientLanguage: 'js', clientFramework: 'jest' }
  // automatically — no extra config needed in pact-js ≥ 12.5
});
```

> [community] Extended verification metadata can expose runtime details (Node.js version, OS) in PactFlow audit logs. For regulated environments, review PactFlow data-retention policies before enabling `publishVerificationResult` on all branches. — GCL-362

## XML Body Matching — Current Status and Workaround

The XML Generators RFC (pact-reference Rust core) reached **completed** status in late 2025. The pact-js binding will expose XML text and attribute generators once the underlying Rust FFI is promoted to stable. Until then, use `withMatchingRules` for content-type-level XML validation:

```typescript
// Workaround: content-type matcher for XML responses until XML generators land in pact-js
import { PactV4, SpecificationVersion } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'ReportConsumer',
  provider: 'LegacyXmlService',
  spec: SpecificationVersion.SPECIFICATION_VERSION_V4,
});

await provider
  .addInteraction()
  .uponReceiving('a request for XML report data')
  .withRequest('GET', '/reports/quarterly')
  .willRespondWith()
  .withStatus(200)
  .withHeader('Content-Type', 'text/xml; charset=utf-8')
  // Use regex matcher on the full body string for now
  .withBody(
    regex(
      /<report>[\s\S]*<quarter>[A-Z0-9]+<\/quarter>[\s\S]*<\/report>/,
      '<report><quarter>Q1-2026</quarter><total>42000</total></report>'
    )
  )
  .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
    const result = await fetchReport(mockServer.url);
    expect(result.quarter).toBe('Q1-2026');
  });
```

**Limitation:** Regex-based XML matching does not validate structure beyond the literal pattern. Add a dedicated XML schema integration test case alongside the contract test case when structural correctness is critical.

> [community] Teams using legacy SOAP or internal XML APIs should maintain a separate integration test layer for schema validation (XSD). Contract test cases cover the consumer's slice of the response; they cannot replace full schema enforcement. — GCL-363

---

## form-urlencoded Body Matching

The `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body matching RFC is active (not yet merged). The current workaround is a `like()` matcher on the full encoded string. **Key pitfall**: URL-encoded key order is not guaranteed across HTTP client implementations.

```typescript
// Current workaround: like() on the encoded body string
// The form() helper is NOT yet available in pact-js
import { like } from '@pact-foundation/pact/src/v3/matchers';

await provider
  .addInteraction()
  .uponReceiving('an OAuth token exchange request')
  .withRequest('POST', '/oauth/token', {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
    // like() matches structure but not exact key ordering
    body: like('grant_type=authorization_code&code=AUTHCODE-001&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fcallback'),
  })
  .willRespondWith()
  .withStatus(200)
  .withJsonBody({ access_token: like('eyJhbGc...'), token_type: 'Bearer' })
  .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
    const token = await exchangeCode(mockServer.url, 'AUTHCODE-001');
    expect(token.token_type).toBe('Bearer');
  });

// FUTURE API (RFC in progress — not yet released):
// body: form({
//   grant_type: equal('authorization_code'),
//   code: like('AUTHCODE-001'),
//   redirect_uri: like('https://app.example.com/callback'),
// })
```

> [community] `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` key order is not specified by RFC 1866 — different HTTP clients serialize keys in different orders. Using `like()` on the full encoded string causes intermittent verification failures when the provider's test HTTP client serializes keys in a different order than the consumer. Normalize to an object comparison using `URLSearchParams` in the provider state setup until the `form()` matcher is available. — GCL-364

## Cycle 70 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 701** — Typed State-Handler Factory to Prevent Provider State String Drift at Compile Time

When both consumer and provider tests are in the same TypeScript monorepo, a typed factory function pattern creates a single source of truth for state strings and their parameter types. A type error surfaces in CI if either side diverges.

```typescript
// shared/pact-state-factory.ts
// Typed state-handler factory: one definition drives both consumer `given()` calls
// and provider `stateHandlers` map keys. Compile-time drift detection.
export interface StateFactory<TParams extends Record<string, unknown> = Record<string, never>> {
  /** Builds the canonical state string and validates params at compile time. */
  build(params: TParams): string;
  /** The state string key for use in `stateHandlers` map — params are validated by the builder. */
  key: (params: TParams) => string;
}

function defineState<TParams extends Record<string, unknown> = Record<string, never>>(
  template: (params: TParams) => string
): StateFactory<TParams> {
  return {
    build: template,
    key: template,
  };
}

// One definition per provider state — exported from the shared module.
export const InventoryStates = {
  skuInStock: defineState<{ sku: string; qty: number }>(
    ({ sku, qty }) => `SKU ${sku} exists with ${qty} units in stock`
  ),
  skuNotFound: defineState<{ sku: string }>(
    ({ sku }) => `SKU ${sku} does not exist`
  ),
  warehouseOffline: defineState<{ warehouseId: string }>(
    ({ warehouseId }) => `Warehouse ${warehouseId} is temporarily offline`
  ),
} as const;
```

```typescript
// packages/order-service/src/inventory.consumer.pact.spec.ts — consumer side
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { InventoryStates } from '../../../shared/pact-state-factory';

const { like, integer } = MatchersV3;
const provider = new PactV3({ consumer: 'OrderService', provider: 'InventoryService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'), port: 8081, logLevel: 'warn' });

it('returns stock for a known SKU', async () => {
  await provider
    // TypeScript error if { sku, qty } shape is wrong
    .given(InventoryStates.skuInStock.build({ sku: 'ABC-123', qty: 10 }))
    .uponReceiving('a stock request for SKU ABC-123')
    .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: '/inventory/ABC-123' })
    .willRespondWith({ status: 200, body: { sku: like('ABC-123'), available: integer(10) } })
    .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new InventoryClient(mockServer.url);
      const result = await client.getStock('ABC-123');
      expect(result.available).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
    });
});
```

```typescript
// packages/inventory-service/src/inventory.provider.pact.spec.ts — provider side
import { VerifierV3, VerifierOptions } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { InventoryStates } from '../../../shared/pact-state-factory';
import { db } from '../db';

const stateHandlers: NonNullable<VerifierOptions['stateHandlers']> = {
  // Computed key — TypeScript error if params shape is wrong
  [InventoryStates.skuInStock.key({ sku: 'ABC-123', qty: 10 })]: async () => {
    await db.seed({ sku: 'ABC-123', available: 10, warehouseId: 'WH-001' });
  },
  [InventoryStates.skuNotFound.key({ sku: 'UNKNOWN-999' })]: async () => {
    await db.clear('UNKNOWN-999');
  },
};
```

Tradeoff: The `defineState` factory enforces a one-to-one mapping between state string template, parameter types, and the handler key — but the computed-key `[InventoryStates.skuInStock.key({ sku: 'ABC-123', qty: 10 })]` syntax in the `stateHandlers` object means only the specific `sku: 'ABC-123', qty: 10` combination is keyed; if the consumer uses a different `qty`, the key is different and no handler matches. The pattern works best when provider states use parameterized templates that are always called with the same canonical example on both sides. For highly dynamic states (arbitrary IDs, arbitrary counts), prefer `fromProviderState()` instead of embedding specific values in the state string.

**Pattern 702** — `can-i-deploy --output json` with `jq` for Structured CI Failure Reporting

The `--output json` flag on `pact-broker can-i-deploy` produces machine-parseable output. This allows CI pipelines to extract and surface specific failure details — which consumer pact failed, which environment, and which provider version it was verified against — rather than raw CLI text.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/can-i-deploy-structured.sh
# Runs can-i-deploy with JSON output and extracts failure details for CI annotations.
# Usage: ./ci/can-i-deploy-structured.sh OrderService "$GIT_COMMIT" staging
set -euo pipefail

PACTICIPANT="${1:?usage: $0 <pacticipant> <version> <environment>}"
VERSION="${2:?}"
ENVIRONMENT="${3:?}"

CID_JSON=$(pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant      "${PACTICIPANT}" \
  --version          "${VERSION}" \
  --to-environment   "${ENVIRONMENT}" \
  --broker-base-url  "${PACT_BROKER_URL}" \
  --broker-token     "${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}" \
  --retry-while-unknown 5 \
  --retry-interval   10 \
  --output json 2>&1 || true)

# Always emit the structured output for CI log parsing
echo "${CID_JSON}"

DEPLOYABLE=$(echo "${CID_JSON}" | jq -r '.summary.deployable // "false"')
if [[ "${DEPLOYABLE}" != "true" ]]; then
  echo ""
  echo "=== can-i-deploy BLOCKED for ${PACTICIPANT}@${VERSION} → ${ENVIRONMENT} ===" >&2
  # Extract which consumer-provider pair failed and why
  echo "${CID_JSON}" | jq -r '
    .matrix[]
    | select(.verificationResult.success == false or .verificationResult == null)
    | "  ❌ \(.consumer.name)@\(.consumer.version) ← \(.provider.name)@\(.provider.version // "unverified"): \(.reason // "no verification result")"
  ' >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "✓ can-i-deploy PASSED: ${PACTICIPANT}@${VERSION} can deploy to ${ENVIRONMENT}"
```

Tradeoff: The `--output json` flag produces a structured `{ summary, matrix }` object — `summary.deployable` is `true`/`false`/`null` (`null` = unknown, i.e. no verification result yet). The `jq` `.matrix[].reason` field is a free-text string from the Broker and its wording may change across Broker versions, making it unsuitable as a stable condition in automated alerting logic. Use `summary.deployable` for the pass/fail gate; use `.matrix[]` fields for diagnostic display only.

**Pattern 703** — `pactfileWriteMode` Decision Guide: `'overwrite'` vs `'update'` vs `'merge'`

pact-js supports three modes for writing pact files to disk. Choosing the wrong mode causes ghost interactions or test-run conflicts in monorepos.

```typescript
// pact-write-modes.ts — annotated examples of all three modes

// Mode 1: 'overwrite' (RECOMMENDED for CI)
// Deletes and rewrites the pact file from scratch on every test run.
// Guarantees: pact file reflects exactly the interactions present in the current test suite.
// Use when: running full consumer test suite in CI; pact dir is cleared between runs.
const providerOverwrite = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'OrderService',
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite',  // CI default: clean slate every run
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

// Mode 2: 'update' (DEFAULT — DANGEROUS in CI without pre-run clean)
// Merges new interactions into any existing pact file.
// Trap: interactions removed from the test suite persist in the file until the file is deleted.
// Use when: intentionally building up a pact file incrementally across a long local session.
const providerUpdate = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'OrderService',
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  pactfileWriteMode: 'update',  // default; switch to 'overwrite' in CI
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

// Mode 3: 'merge' (for split-file suites)
// Same as 'update' but also de-duplicates interactions by (description, providerState) key.
// Use when: a single provider's pact is split across multiple consumer test files
//           that run in separate Jest workers — each file appends its interactions
//           without clobbering the others.
// Caveat: still accumulates ghost interactions if tests are deleted; pair with
//         a globalSetup rm -rf pacts/ to clear the directory before each full run.
const providerMerge = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'OrderService',
  provider: 'InventoryService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  pactfileWriteMode: 'merge',  // multi-file suite; combine with pre-run cleanup
  logLevel: 'warn',
});
```

```typescript
// jest.globalSetup.ts — clear pacts directory before each full consumer test run
// Used with pactfileWriteMode: 'merge' to prevent ghost interaction accumulation.
import { rm } from 'fs/promises';
import { existsSync } from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const pactsDir = path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts');
  if (existsSync(pactsDir)) {
    await rm(pactsDir, { recursive: true, force: true });
    console.log('[pact globalSetup] Cleared pacts directory before test run');
  }
}
```

**Decision table:**

| Scenario | Recommended mode | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Full consumer suite in CI | `'overwrite'` | Clean slate — no ghost interactions |
| Single consumer test file | `'overwrite'` | Simplest; no state to carry over |
| Split consumer suite across Jest workers | `'merge'` + `globalSetup` cleanup | Workers append without collision; cleanup prevents ghost accumulation |
| Local incremental development | `'update'` | Append new interactions without losing others during iteration |
| Default if not set | `'update'` | Change to `'overwrite'` in CI via env-conditional config |

**Pattern 704** — `pact-broker create-environment` as Infrastructure-as-Code Step

The Pact Broker's environment API (`create-environment`, `can-i-deploy --to-environment`, `record-deployment`) requires environments to be pre-created. Skipping this in IaC setup causes silent `record-deployment` failures. This pattern captures the environment bootstrap as a Terraform-style shell script committed to the infra repo.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# infra/pact/bootstrap-environments.sh
# Creates Pact Broker environments for each deployment tier.
# Run once per Broker instance (CI/CD setup, Terraform null_resource, or manually).
# Safe to re-run — existing environments are returned without error.
set -euo pipefail

BROKER_URL="${PACT_BROKER_URL:?PACT_BROKER_URL required}"
TOKEN="${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN:?PACT_BROKER_TOKEN required}"

# Environments to create — add/remove tiers to match your deployment pipeline.
ENVIRONMENTS=(development staging production)

for ENV in "${ENVIRONMENTS[@]}"; do
  echo "Creating environment: ${ENV}"
  # pact-broker create-environment is idempotent — exits 0 if already exists
  pact-broker create-environment \
    --name          "${ENV}" \
    --display-name  "${ENV^}" \
    --broker-base-url "${BROKER_URL}" \
    --broker-token    "${TOKEN}" || {
      echo "Warning: environment '${ENV}' may already exist (exit code $?). Continuing."
    }
done

echo "Pact Broker environments bootstrapped: ${ENVIRONMENTS[*]}"
```

```typescript
// infra/pact/verify-environments.ts — CI pre-flight check
// Verifies all required environments exist in the Broker before a deployment pipeline starts.
// Fails fast with a clear error if an environment was accidentally deleted.
interface BrokerEnvironment {
  name: string;
  displayName: string;
  createdAt: string;
}

const REQUIRED_ENVIRONMENTS = ['development', 'staging', 'production'] as const;

async function verifyPactEnvironments(brokerUrl: string, token: string): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(`${brokerUrl}/environments`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, Accept: 'application/hal+json' },
  });
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Pact Broker API error ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  const json = await response.json() as { _embedded: { environments: BrokerEnvironment[] } };
  const existingNames = new Set(json._embedded.environments.map((e) => e.name));

  const missing = REQUIRED_ENVIRONMENTS.filter((env) => !existingNames.has(env));
  if (missing.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(
      `Pact Broker is missing required environments: ${missing.join(', ')}.\n` +
      `Run: bash infra/pact/bootstrap-environments.sh to create them.`
    );
  }
  console.log(`✓ All Pact Broker environments verified: ${REQUIRED_ENVIRONMENTS.join(', ')}`);
}

// Called as a pre-flight step in the CD pipeline
verifyPactEnvironments(
  process.env.PACT_BROKER_URL!,
  process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN!
).catch((err) => { console.error(err.message); process.exit(1); });
```

Tradeoff: The `create-environment` CLI call is idempotent but not fully atomic — if two CD pipeline runs race to create the same environment simultaneously, the second call returns a 409 conflict. The shell script above treats non-zero exits from `create-environment` as warnings (not failures) to handle this race. In production IaC, use a Terraform `null_resource` with `triggers = { always_run = timestamp() }` to serialize environment creation, or manage environments via the PactFlow Terraform provider if your team uses PactFlow.

**Pattern 705** — `arrayContaining` Diagnostic Improvement: Labelled Subset Assertions

The `arrayContaining` matcher from `MatchersV3` produces terse failure output when provider verification fails: it reports only "Array did not contain expected elements" without identifying which elements were missing. The following wrapper pattern adds labelled output for easier CI debugging.

```typescript
// shared/pact-array-diagnostics.ts
// Wraps arrayContaining with a labelled helper that adds a comment annotation
// to the interaction so the Broker UI shows which elements were expected.
import { MatchersV3, PactV4 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';

const { arrayContaining, string } = MatchersV3;

// Annotated arrayContaining: adds a Pact V4 .withComment() to the interaction
// describing which elements were expected. Works only with the V4 interaction DSL.
// Usage: pair with .withComment() on the parent interaction (V4 only).
export function labelledArrayContaining<T>(
  label: string,
  items: T[]
): { _label: string; matcher: ReturnType<typeof arrayContaining> } {
  return {
    _label: label,
    matcher: arrayContaining(items),
  };
}

// Example usage — V4 interaction with labelled arrayContaining and comment annotation:
const provider = new PactV4({
  consumer: 'SearchUI',
  provider: 'CatalogService',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
  logLevel: 'warn',
});

describe('SearchUI → CatalogService: permission roles contract', () => {
  it('response contains at minimum the read and write roles', async () => {
    const expectedRoles = labelledArrayContaining(
      'required permission roles',
      [string('read'), string('write')]
    );

    await provider
      .addInteraction()
      .given('user has read and write roles')
      .uponReceiving('a GET /me/roles request')
      // V4 .withComment() is visible in Pact Broker UI and improves failure diagnostics
      .withComment(`arrayContaining checks: ${expectedRoles._label} — ${JSON.stringify(expectedRoles.matcher)}`)
      .withRequest('GET', '/me/roles')
      .willRespondWith(200, (builder) => {
        builder.jsonBody({
          userId: string('user-001'),
          roles: expectedRoles.matcher,
        });
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const result = await fetch(`${mockServer.url}/me/roles`).then((r) => r.json());
        expect(Array.isArray(result.roles)).toBe(true);
        expect(result.roles).toContain('read');
        expect(result.roles).toContain('write');
      });
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: The `labelledArrayContaining` wrapper adds the expected element list as a V4 `.withComment()` annotation, which is stored in the pact file and surfaced in the Broker UI's interaction view — but it does not change how the matching rule engine reports failures at verification time. The underlying `arrayContaining` failure message from the Rust FFI core remains terse. The improvement is in pre-failure documentation (Broker UI context) rather than post-failure diagnostic text. For clearer verification failures, add a provider-side test assertion that manually checks each expected element: `expect(result.roles).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining(['read', 'write']))` — this produces Jest's standard `Expected array: ...` diff format.

### Community Gotchas

**GCL-365** — `pactfileWriteMode` Default Is `'update'`, Not `'overwrite'` — Ghost Interactions Accumulate in CI Caches
Why this matters: pact-js uses `pactfileWriteMode: 'update'` by default, which merges each test run into the existing on-disk file rather than regenerating it. In CI systems with workspace caching (GitHub Actions `actions/cache`, Nx Cloud, Turborepo remote cache), the `pacts/` directory may be restored from a cache key that includes a now-deleted interaction. The next CI run merges new interactions into the cached file — the deleted interaction persists and is published to the Broker. Provider verification then fails on a test case no consumer code references. The failure is invisible in the consumer codebase: the deleted test left no trace, so engineers investigate the provider looking for a regression that does not exist.
Fix: Set `pactfileWriteMode: 'overwrite'` in all CI configurations. Add a `jest globalSetup` or pipeline pre-step that runs `rm -rf pacts/` before the consumer test suite. Explicitly exclude the `pacts/` directory from all CI caching configurations (add `pacts/**` to `.gitignore` and to the cache exclusion list). For monorepos, add a Turborepo `outputs` entry of `["!pacts/**"]` to prevent the pacts directory from being cached as a build artifact.

---

**GCL-366** — `can-i-deploy` Returns `null` Deployability When the Provider Has Never Published Verification Results for the Environment
Why this matters: `pact-broker can-i-deploy --to-environment staging` returns `deployable: null` (unknown) rather than `false` when the provider has never run a verification tagged to the `staging` environment. Teams that set `--retry-while-unknown 0` (or omit the flag, which defaults to no retries) treat `null` as a deployment blocker and incorrectly conclude that their pact pipeline is broken. The real cause is that the provider CI is configured to publish verification results only with `--to-environment production`, omitting `staging` from `record-deployment` calls. The consumer's `can-i-deploy` gate can never receive a `true` result because the compatibility matrix for `staging` is permanently empty.
Fix: Audit the provider CI pipeline to confirm that `pact-broker record-deployment` is called for every environment the consumer gates against. Add a CI notification step that fires when `can-i-deploy` times out after `--retry-while-unknown` retries, distinguishing a "timeout/unknown" exit from a "verified incompatible" exit: the JSON output field `summary.deployable` is `null` vs `false`. Route "unknown" timeouts to a Slack alert for manual investigation rather than treating them identically to "incompatible" failures.

---

**GCL-367** — `stateHandlers` Receive `params` as `Record<string, unknown>` But TypeScript Typed Handlers Expect a Specific Interface — Silent `undefined` Access
Why this matters: When a consumer uses `given('order exists', { orderId: 'ORD-001' })` and the provider declares `stateHandlers` with `async ({ orderId }) => { ... }`, TypeScript infers the parameter destructuring as `{ orderId: unknown }`. If the consumer's state string uses a different param name (e.g., `order_id` vs `orderId`), the destructuring resolves `orderId` to `undefined` at runtime — and TypeScript does not warn, because `Record<string, unknown>` allows any key. The state handler proceeds with `orderId === undefined`, which typically triggers a database error or a lookup miss that manifests as a confusing body mismatch in verification output rather than a state setup failure.
Fix: Use typed state-handler parameter interfaces with runtime validation: `const { orderId } = params as { orderId: string }; if (typeof orderId !== 'string') throw new Error(\`stateHandlers['order exists']: expected orderId:string, got ${typeof orderId}\`);`. Centralise state parameter types in the shared `pact-state-factory.ts` module (Pattern 701 above) and add a provider-side unit test that calls each state handler with its expected parameter object, asserting the database seed call received the correct arguments. This catches naming inconsistencies between consumer and provider at the unit test level before they reach the Pact verification step.

---

**GCL-368** — Provider Test Server Port Leak Causes `EADDRINUSE` on Repeated Local Runs Without `afterAll` Cleanup
Why this matters: When a provider verification test starts an HTTP server in `beforeAll` and the test suite is interrupted (Ctrl-C, timeout, uncaught promise rejection in a state handler), the `afterAll` cleanup that calls `server.close()` never runs. The next local test run attempts to bind to the same port and fails with `Error: listen EADDRINUSE :::3001`. Engineers restart by changing the `PORT` env var to an unused port, accumulating phantom processes over a workday. In Docker-based CI, the same behaviour prevents port reuse across parallel pipeline runs if the Docker network is not isolated per job.
Fix: Register a `process.on('SIGINT', cleanup)` and `process.on('SIGTERM', cleanup)` handler in the provider test file's global scope, where `cleanup` calls `server.close()` and resolves a shared promise that the `afterAll` awaits. In Jest, add `--forceExit` to the provider test command to ensure Jest terminates the process (and triggers OS-level socket cleanup) even when `afterAll` does not complete. In GitHub Actions, add `timeout-minutes: 5` to the provider verification step so interrupted runs release Docker network ports before the next job starts.

---

**GCL-369** — `enablePending: true` Without `providerVersionBranch` Does Not Graduate Pending Pacts — All Interactions Stay Pending Forever
Why this matters: The Pact Broker graduates a pending pact to "verified" only when the provider publishes a successful verification result that includes a `providerVersionBranch`. If `providerVersionBranch` is omitted from the `VerifierV3` options, the broker receives unbranchable verification results and cannot graduate any interaction. With `enablePending: true` active, all interactions remain permanently pending — failing interactions produce only advisory warnings, never build failures, regardless of how broken the contract is. This creates a false green CI state: the provider team sees zero failures while all consumer interactions are silently unverifiable. Unlike GCL-359 (which covers the general `providerVersionBranch` omission case), this gotcha specifically surfaces when `enablePending` and `providerVersionBranch` are misconfigured together in the same upgrade.
Fix: Treat `providerVersionBranch` as a required field, not optional: add a startup guard that throws if `GIT_BRANCH` (or your CI's equivalent) is not set. Run `pact-broker list-latest-pact-versions --provider InventoryService` after the first fixed verification run to confirm that interactions are showing as "verified" rather than "pending" in the broker matrix. Add a periodic CI check (e.g., a weekly job) that queries the broker for any pact that has been in pending status for more than 30 days and files a team alert, because permanently-pending interactions indicate a systemic configuration problem rather than a feature in progress.
